articles.title_orig: Dow jumps 500 points as solid earnings, falling crude oil stir rebound: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Dow jumps 500 points as solid earnings, falling crude oil stir rebound: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
Get Mike Santoli's Market Memo in your inbox first. SUBSCRIBE HERE
In a previous life, when I routinely shut down New York City bars, the end of Daylight Saving Time was an annual bonus, as 2am on a Saturday night instantly became 1am, leaving three more hours until closing time.
The financial markets now are undergoing several forms of late-cycle unease, and Wall Street is now looking for earnings season and the passage of the midterm elections to turn back the clock before last call.
To be clear, this remains a bull market, the S&P 500 's uptrend unbroken, with constant rotations between AI tech and remainder of the market fitfully supporting the tape, with pullbacks limited to 3% for half a year.
Still, the index is now chopping around a flattish 50-day moving average at levels first reached 11 weeks ago, the AI-hardware cohort has badly broken stride, bank stocks are trading poorly off their results, and credit markets are getting colicky.
Late last week, the urgent selling in semiconductors and data-center equities and debt resembled the sort of forced-unwind rhythms from July, when a big upstart tech hedge fund was in the process of being all but liquidated.
A tentative bounce in semiconductor stocks Monday was minimally reassuring, in that it meant we didn't get the further disorderly purge many had braced for over the weekend (when S&P 500 "perpetual" futures on Hyperliquid had a sudden head-fake drop late Saturday).
Jason Hunter, technical strategist at JP Morgan, sets out the crucial question for a market sending mixed signals:
"With the bearish seasonal window now closing, we are left wondering if the market is in the terminal phase of a sequence of rolling corrections ahead of a typical late-year rally. Or are the plentiful amounts of bearish internal, momentum, and intra-market divergences that have formed as the S&P 500 index has decelerated below longer-term channel resistance setting the market up for a larger and more correlated setback?"
He leans toward a more cautious interpretation, keeping the S&P 500 on a short leash that extends about 2.5% lower to 7500, a break of which would lose the tape the benefit of the doubt.
Based on precedent and circumstance, the market "should" be setting up for a comeback that could reset the clock in bulls' favor. The fourth quarter after a midterm election year, historically, is overwhelmingly positive. Earnings growth projected to exceed a 20% year-over-year growth rate again this quarter can hardly be viewed as anything but a positive at least to bolster the fundamental case.
Still, against most probabilities, 2018 happened. By which I mean a 19% S&P 500 peak-to-trough decline in the fourth quarter of a midterm-election year, one that saw total S&P 500 earnings grow by more than 20%.
The 2018 tailspin had followed a massive momentum crescendo and reversal several months earlier, which gave way to an erratic tape that couldn't absorb what seemed at the time relatively unthreatening Federal Reserve tightening actions.
Financial conditions have now been tightening by means of higher Treasury yields, somewhat wider corporate-credit spreads, an uptick in volatility and a stronger U.S. dollar.
It's become common to hear investors insist that "the market is doing the Fed's tightening for it," suggesting Chairman Kevin Warsh himself should show restraint in further hiking rates despite the recent upturn in inflation. Sure, but the reason the markets are tightening is, in part, because Warsh himself expressed resolve in fighting inflation and investors therefore believe he'll take short-term rates up a bit more.
How Warsh treats these market shifts after next week's Fed meeting is another node of disagreement on the Street.
Bank of America economist Aditya Bhave says the markets are testing the Fed's pain threshold with the Nasdaq retreating 5% and credit spreads flaring a bit. The market has taken recent Fedspeak to suggest very low chances of an October rate hike, even though Warsh himself has decried forward guidance and said the Fed shouldn't suppress normal market volatility. Bhave is maintaining his non-consensus prediction for an October hike, conceding it's a close call.
Morgan Stanley equity strategist Mike Wilson takes the other side on the Fed's response to the recent tensing up of markets: "We think some acknowledgement of this tightening by Warsh would be well received by rate-sensitive areas that have already derated notably. Conversely, an indifference to this tightening may invoke memories of Powell's 2018 'auto-pilot' remarks in reference to that tightening episode."
The "de-rating" and "de-risking" process has surely been notable in recent weeks, with small and cyclical stocks under significant valuation pressure and hedge funds aggressively repositioning out of tech.
Is it enough to enliven buyers into or after the election?
Ned Davis Research thematic strategist Pat Tschosik notes his firm's proprietary market-breadth reading Big Mo Tape tentatively turning higher from oversold readings. "If Big Tech disappoints on Q3 earnings, we may get a full market washout and Big Mo could head even lower like it did in October 2023. Perhaps this is what is needed to set up for a post-midterm-election rally into yearend."
John Kolovos of Macro Risk Advisors sees a similar level to JPMorgan's as the market's breaking point, while evaluating his sentiment indicator.
Kolovos on the latest reading: "A noticeable sentiment reset is underway on the heels of the AI trade unwind and tightening financial conditions.  The good news is that bullish sentiment is finally starting to wash out, which should set the stage for a year-end rally. However, a break below the mid-September lows on the S&P 500 near 7,500 would warn that something more than a routine pullback is unfolding."
-There's something of a paradox at work – or a collective investor blind spot - when the bond market is finally offering relatively safe income after many years of meager yields and yet people continue to rush for the engineered income delivered by options-selling ETFs. This CNBC.com piece offers a thorough, smart rundown of these strategies, complete with warnings of tax pitfalls. This Bloomberg report details a more aggressive approach through funds many investors don't quite understand, while introducing me to the community of self-styled "dividend nomads."
-Anthropic's proposal to place 5% of its equity into a "public benefit fund" to help groups potentially disadvantaged by AI's propagation and Elon Musk's stated offer to give one of his SpaceX shares to every American child via Trump Accounts suggest that anxiety over AI economic disruption is going from simmer to boil.
We can cynically observe that such efforts also hype these companies' world-changing potency, a form of marketing through scare-mongering sheathed in generosity.  But the concern over AI's impact on current worker groups is well-placed, even if ultimately society adapts around step-function technological change. The best hedge against AI-powered capital overtaking labor is arguably to own more capital, whether through the S&P 500 or other vehicles.
Or one could raise the value of one's human capital, through training or becoming excellent at something. This has always been Warren Buffett's answer for how one should become inflation-resistant, as he detailed at Berkshire Hathaway's annual meeting a few years ago , at the height of the pandemic inflation surge.
Bull markets can keep rolling for a long while after they've become fully embraced and stocks are no longer cheap. But I find myself cataloguing various ways that the cushions against adverse surprises are getting worn pretty flat.
Here's the running tally of investors' collective cash holdings as a percentage of total margin debt. It's running well below the levels of the year 2000 at this point.

Russia was set to gain most if the trilateral meeting took place, experts said, as the summit would be a potent symbol that the country’s international isolation was ending and of its great-power status. articles.title_orig: China slams US ban on DeepSeek AI over security concerns
articles.title_zh: China slams US ban on DeepSeek AI over security concerns
articles.content_orig:
Boeing unveiled a new artificial intelligence-powered platform Tuesday designed to help airlines anticipate aircraft maintenance needs, identify emerging risks and make faster operational decisions using data collected across their fleets.
The platform, called Dataliner, was developed in partnership with Microsoft and uses AI to combine aircraft maintenance records, operational information and Boeing's engineering expertise to give airlines a more complete picture of their fleets.
Built using Microsoft's Azure AI Foundry and other technologies, Dataliner aims to help airlines move beyond analyzing individual aircraft to identifying maintenance trends and potential problems across entire fleets.
"Airlines have more data available to them than ever before, but turning that data into meaningful action remains a challenge," said Lindsey Douglas, vice president of Cabin, Modifications, Maintenance and Digital Services at Boeing Global Services.
Douglas said the platform will help customers "anticipate maintenance needs, identify emerging risks and take timely action."
Boeing said airlines will retain control over their data, including what information they share, while the platform uses encryption, access controls and monitoring to protect sensitive aviation information.
Dataliner will also support the development of new Boeing digital services, including an AI-powered tool for airline technical operations and aircraft lifecycle planning.
China launched a new state-owned data enterprise Tuesday aimed at strengthening its position in the global artificial intelligence race as Beijing moves to expand the development and use of data resources critical to advancing AI technology.
The National Data Group, headquartered in Xiongan, roughly 60 miles southwest of Beijing, will serve as a national platform to promote data sharing across industries and regions, according to state media.
The group will also work with various stakeholders to develop China's data economy, explore new business models and expand the market, state broadcaster CCTV reported.
Chinese Vice Premier Ding Xuexiang attended Tuesday's inauguration ceremony, saying the group's establishment was important for capitalizing on opportunities in artificial intelligence and strengthening China's competitive edge, according to state media.
The announcement comes amid intensifying technological competition between Washington and Beijing, including a recent U.S. ban on Chinese AI startup DeepSeek's products across federal civilian agencies over national security concerns.
China established its National Data Administration in 2023 to oversee data policy, while the new National Data Group will focus on market operations and putting data resources to use.
Reuters contributed to this report.
Artificial intelligence may be transforming the job market, but nearly half of U.S. employers believe the technology will make college degrees more valuable over the next five years, according to a new Gallup poll.
The Gallup-Lumina Foundation survey found that 48% of employers expect AI to increase the importance of college degrees, compared with 26% who believe the technology will make them less valuable.
The findings suggest higher education remains a priority for hiring managers despite growing concerns about AI's impact on the workforce.
About 80% of employers said they prefer hiring candidates with college degrees, even for positions that do not require one.
The survey also revealed a divide between employers and the broader public over the value of higher education.
While 60% of employers expressed a great deal or quite a lot of confidence in higher education, just 38% of U.S. adults reported the same in a separate Gallup survey conducted in June.
The findings are based on an August survey of 2,500 U.S. hiring decision-makers.
Pharmaceutical giant AstraZeneca is teaming up with tech powerhouse Oracle to use artificial intelligence to identify patients for clinical trials and monitor potential safety risks, in a move aimed at speeding up drug development and improving medical research.
The partnership will combine AstraZeneca's drug development expertise with Oracle's AI technology and healthcare data capabilities to help researchers match patients with clinical trials and identify potential safety concerns.
The collaboration will initially focus on cancer, cardiovascular and respiratory diseases, immunology and rare diseases, with the technology potentially helping doctors diagnose serious illnesses earlier.
AstraZeneca CEO Pascal Soriot said the partnership could help researchers and healthcare providers improve patient care through AI-driven technology.
"We can help clinicians identify patients sooner, optimize clinical trials, and generate evidence continuously across the lifecycle of a medicine," Soriot said in a statement.
The first project will focus on hypertension research in Abu Dhabi, in partnership with UAE-based healthcare company M42.
Patient recruitment remains a major obstacle in clinical research, with enrollment delays often extending trial timelines and driving up development costs.
AstraZeneca has also faced clinical trial setbacks, including delays involving a breast cancer treatment and the failure of a nerve disorder drug, raising concerns about its drug development efforts, according to Reuters.
The companies have signed a non-binding agreement and have not disclosed financial terms.
The partnership comes as AstraZeneca seeks to expand its drug portfolio and reach more than $80 billion in annual revenue by 2030.
Reuters contributed to this report.
China fired back at the Trump administration Tuesday after the U.S. government ordered federal civilian agencies to remove Chinese artificial intelligence startup DeepSeek's products from their systems, citing national security concerns and the risk that Beijing could gain access to sensitive American data.
The Department of Homeland Security ordered agencies to remove DeepSeek products and services, including third-party technology developed using its AI models, and prohibited future purchases, according to a notice made public Monday in the Federal Register.
The order, issued in July, warned that DeepSeek's AI models "present multiple threat vectors," citing concerns that the company's China-based servers could potentially expose sensitive U.S. data to Chinese authorities.
Beijing criticized the ban, with Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning accusing Washington of politicizing technology.
"China consistently opposes the overstretching of the concept of national security and the politicizing of science, technology, economic and trade issues," Mao told reporters Tuesday.
Mao added that Beijing would "resolutely safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese companies."
DeepSeek did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital’s request for comment.
The dispute comes ahead of a planned November meeting between President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping, where AI is expected to be on the agenda.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.
Covered by: Stephen Sorace

articles.title_orig: Walmart rolls out new bundle combining Walmart+, Sam’s Club Plus
articles.title_zh: Walmart rolls out new bundle combining Walmart+, Sam’s Club Plus
articles.content_orig:
LSEG head of consumer research Jharonne Marti discusses the mind of the consumer and the Walmart overreaction on 'Making Money.'
Walmart announced Tuesday it is rolling out a new membership bundle that gives shoppers access to both Walmart+ and Sam’s Club Plus for $120 a year, nearly $100 less than purchasing the two memberships separately.
The bundle works out to the equivalent of $10 per month, though Walmart said it will only be available as an annual membership and will not include a monthly option or free trial.
Walmart CEO John Furner told FOX Business that the retail giant wanted to roll out the combined membership ahead of the holiday season, when many households are looking for ways to save both money and time.
"It does help at a time when we do see some customers showing some signs of pressure," Furner said, pointing in particular to higher energy costs.
SAM’S CLUB EXPANDS THANKSGIVING MEAL, KEEPING COST UNDER $10 A PERSON AS INFLATION WEIGHS ON CONSUMERS
Walmart said the combined membership costs almost $100 less annually than paying for Walmart+ and Sam’s Club Plus separately. (Christopher Dilts/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
The launch comes after Walmart reported continued growth across its membership and e-commerce businesses in its most recent quarterly results in August.
During the company's second-quarter fiscal 2027 earnings call on Aug. 20, Furner said membership fee revenue increased 17% to an all-time high.
"Marketplace, fulfillment services, membership, advertising and other commerce solutions are strengthening our business, and they are improving the economics of the company," he said at the time.
WALMART DOUBLES DOWN ON PLEDGE AGAINST AI-POWERED PERSONALIZED PRICING
Furner also said Walmart+ membership grew by double digits during the quarter, while Sam's Club membership posted growth in the U.S., China and Mexico.
He told FOX Business that the bundle is designed to appeal across income levels.
WALMART EXPANDS DRONE DELIVERY TO 2 MAJOR US CITIES
Walmart+ currently costs $98 for the standard annual plan, while Sam's Club Plus costs $120 a year.
The new bundle rivals Amazon Prime, which costs $139 annually.
Members will receive the benefits of both programs, including free delivery from Walmart and Sam’s Club, access to Sam’s Club locations and member-only pricing, a choice between Peacock and Paramount+, gas discounts and 2% Sam’s Cash on eligible purchases, according to the retailer.
Furner said Walmart aims to have the bundle encourage existing Walmart+ members to shop at Sam’s Club and also appeal to consumers who currently have memberships elsewhere.
"We're deciding to do this from a position of strength and momentum," Furner said.
Annual Walmart+ members can add Sam’s Club Plus for an additional $22 per year, while existing Sam’s Club members can upgrade to Plus for $60 and receive Walmart+ at no additional cost.
Current Sam’s Club Plus members will be able to activate Walmart+ at no additional charge.
Inflation accelerated in September, with higher energy costs helping push consumer prices higher. (Scott Olson/Getty Images)
Walmart also said U.S. field associates at Walmart and Sam’s Club will receive access to both memberships as part of their employee benefits.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The new offering comes as consumers continue to contend with higher prices. Inflation climbed 3.7% in September from a year earlier, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics' Consumer Price Index. Gasoline prices rose more than 34% over the past year, while grocery prices climbed 1.8%.

articles.title_orig: Salesforce announces $5.66 billion deal for Braze, sending BRZE stock soaring 50%
articles.title_zh: Salesforce announces $5.66 billion deal for Braze, sending BRZE stock soaring 50%
articles.content_orig:
Shares of Salesforce slipped roughly 1% on Tuesday morning, after the company announced an agreement to buy customer engagement platform Braze for about $5.66 billion.
Under the deal, holders of Braze Class A common stock will get $47.50 in cash per share. The transaction is expected to close in fiscal 2028, subject to shareholder and regulatory approvals, according to a Salesforce blog .
Braze shares closed at $30.04 on Monday. The stock skyrocketed more than 50% on Tuesday after a brief halt premarket following the news. The company makes artificial intelligence marketing tools to manage customer data and messaging.
"Salesforce shares our commitment to marketers, and we'll continue building as Braze and investing in the Braze community of customers and partners who built this company with us," Bill Magnuson, CEO of Braze, said in a statement. "Salesforce's platform will help us innovate faster and together we'll help marketers around the world build deeper, more lasting relationships with their customers."
The latest deal comes just months after Salesforce announced it would buy AI customer service platform Fin for about $3.6 billion, in a move meant to bolster the company's agentic AI offerings for enterprises.
In August, Salesforce and Anthropic announced an expanded partnership , including a new plugin called "Claudeforce" with pre-built sales skills for salespeople to better compose emails, update records and more with the frontier lab's model.

articles.title_orig: Zelenskyy meets with Trump envoys as U.S. blasts ‘scandalous’ accusations on withdrawn support
articles.title_zh: Zelenskyy meets with Trump envoys as U.S. blasts ‘scandalous’ accusations on withdrawn support
articles.content_orig:
U.S. envoys were meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Norway on Tuesday, as Kyiv scrambled to respond to an American pressure campaign that has been allied with moves aimed at courting the Kremlin.
President Donald Trump’s negotiators, son-in-law Jared Kushner and special envoy Steve Witkoff, have so far had little success finding a diplomatic solution to the war . Their latest meeting comes with Washington’s backing in doubt as Kyiv accused the U.S. of withdrawing support crucial to its defense against Russia — a suggestion that Secretary of State Marco Rubio called “scandalous.”
Witkoff had been set to meet with Zelenskyy in Oslo, with Kushner joining via videoconference, the Norwegian government said earlier. Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre and Finnish President Alexander Stubb was also joining the talks, it added.
Officials from the U.S. and Ukraine had been expected to meet in Norway this week for another round of negotiations, sources familiar with the matter told NBC News, as a series of recent actions by Trump in favor of Russia left both Congress and U.S. allies questioning U.S. mediation efforts.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters he hoped that it would be possible for Trump’s envoys to hold a meeting in Russia “in the near future,” though he gave no firm indication on when this might be.
Trump has waived sanctions and agreed a diesel deal with Russia, in an apparent bid to lower fuel prices ahead of the Midterm elections. He called Monday for Zelenskyy to “get somebody else to negotiate,” his latest rebuke of the Ukrainian president.
Trump also appeared to downplay the impact of Russian attacks on Ukraine, a near-daily reality for the last 4 ½ years that have killed scores of civilians and flattened towns.
“Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine,” Trump told reporters. “They haven’t been doing much.”
It was the latest public sign of his shift away from Ukraine.
Kyiv said it had once again received no early warning from the U.S. before the capital came under attack by Russian ballistic missiles on Sunday, the third time in recent days.
In addition to the withholding of intelligence, Ukraine said it was still facing speed restrictions on Starshield, the military version of the SpaceX service, with no explanation from the American side.
“All of this suggests that some political decision has been made to slow down support for us,” Zelenskyy said Monday in a virtual address to a bipartisan Congressional delegation. He also said the U.S. was delaying the delivery of crucial ballistic missile interceptors, and that Ukraine has nearly run out of its supplies.
Zelenskyy said early Tuesday he held “a substantive conversation” with Rubio, focusing on missile interceptors, early warnings of ballistic attacks and Starshield restrictions. He thanked Rubio and “everyone in America who supports fair approaches.”
Rubio told reporters later that he told Zelenskyy in the 45-minute call that nothing had changed in U.S. support for Ukraine.
“There’s nothing being deliberately denied to Ukraine,” he added, speaking at the start of a trip to India.
When it comes to missile interceptors, Rubio said the U.S. has to strike a delicate balance between its obligations to other partners and its own requirements when it comes to what he called “the most in-demand product” in the defense industry right now.
“When a country doesn’t get interceptors from the United States, it’s not because we are denying,” he added. “We have our own needs too.”
Ukrainian officials including Zelenskyy have made clear their accusation that the U.S. has imposed restrictions that have disrupted military operations and hampered Ukraine’s ability to intercept Russian missiles, making the attacks more deadly.
“That’s scandalous, that’s outrageous, that’s just simply not true. That’s not accurate,” Rubio said Tuesday.
Officials in the eastern Kharkiv region shared images Monday of a dead child in a stroller — a one-year-old girl they said was killed alongside her mother in a Russian attack on a public park in the region.
“ The world has enough strength to stop the war. That strength must finally be used — against the murderers,” Zelenskyy said in a post decrying the strike.
Yuliya Talmazan is a reporter for NBC News Digital, based in London.
Abigail Williams is a producer and reporter for NBC News covering the State Department.

articles.title_orig: Russia is working 'closely' with Iran as Qatar says US-Tehran talks are still on
articles.title_zh: Russia is working 'closely' with Iran as Qatar says US-Tehran talks are still on
articles.content_orig:
Al Araby Al Jadeed is reporting that Qatar and Pakistan have put a “compromise proposal” in front of Washington and Tehran that meets the demands of both sides. The key detail is that the plan, presented to Iranian officials today by Pakistan’s army chief, reportedly already has American sign-off and some prior Iranian approval.
The same outlet cites a source saying a breakthrough to halt escalation between Washington and Tehran is expected to be announced this week. Mediators are still working to narrow the remaining points of contention.
The market reaction is modest with crude is down about $1 per barrel since the headlines hit a half-hour ago. Naturally, traders are reluctant to trade on any Iran headlines, particularly coming from a questionable source.
Still, the structure is creative. Paying out interest rather than principal lets both sides claim a win. Tehran gets cash, and Washington can say the core funds stay frozen. A quiet IAEA visit is the kind of face-saving inspection that has to happen before anything bigger can, though the immediate leaking of a 'secret' visit isn't going to build trust. If Pakistan’s army chief is personally carrying the paper, it’s being taken seriously at a high level.
For oil, a real de-escalation removes some of the risk premium tied to Hormuz and the region.  Watch for official statements from Washington, Tehran or Doha but it's going to be a slow-moving process in any event. Obvsiously WTI above $100 and brent above $110 are reasons for the US to seek a deal ahead of the Nov 3 midterms.

articles.title_orig: It’s Not Just France. Europe’s Political Center Is Crumbling.
articles.title_zh: It’s Not Just France. Europe’s Political Center Is Crumbling.
articles.content_orig:
Anger over the cost of living and pressure on public services has brought hundreds of thousands of protesters onto streets across several European countries, with grievances ranging from expensive housing to poor conditions in schools and universities.
France saw the largest demonstrations at the weekend, with more than 500,000 people marching. Most protested peacefully, but some looted and vandalized shops, set fire to city halls and attacked police officers.
Separate protests also took place in Italy, Spain, Portugal and Albania on Saturday and Sunday. Their immediate triggers differed, although high fuel and energy costs formed part of the backdrop in several countries. The wars in Iran and Ukraine have pushed diesel prices sharply higher across the continent.
There's no one "single trigger" for the riots, Capital Economics' Chief Europe Economist Andrew Kenningham told CNBC. The increase in energy costs may be playing a role, but the increase is smaller than in 2022, at the onset of the Russia-Ukraine war, when there were no comparable violent protests, he added.
Nevertheless, the demonstrations pose a shared challenge for governments: how to improve living conditions and maintain public services while supporting households and keeping strained public finances in check.
The demonstrations in France began last month when high school students criticized poor schooling conditions, including shoddy facilities and teacher shortages. They have since evolved into broader protests over living standards and declining public services.
In Spain, housing protests began in September after an 87-year-old woman, Maricarmen Abascal, was evicted following a 230% rent increase by an investment fund. She died a fortnight later.
Thousands of protesters also took to the streets in Portugal on Saturday to demonstrate against soaring housing costs and the cost of living.
"People obviously are protesting on the cost of living with diesel and fuel prices, but mainly on housing costs, which have been increasing substantially all over Europe, but also particularly in Portugal," Miranda Sarmento, Portugal's minister of state and finance, said Monday.
In Albania, protesters were angry about poor university conditions and high tuition fees, and called for the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama. Some threw Molotov cocktails and other objects at the police and set fire to cars and litter bins.
In Italy, a march in central Milan on Saturday over living costs also ended violently, with rioters attacking the police with stones and paving blocks and setting fire to barricades.
"The underlying problem is that politicians are not able to offer hope of a better life for many Europeans because the economy is growing only slowly and governments have built up huge debts, leaving them little scope to support higher public spending or to cut taxes," Capital Economics' Kenningham said.
The escalation of violence in France in particular is due to a "conjugation of different elements," said Douglas Yates, a professor at the American Graduate School in Paris.
"This was a storm that turned into a hurricane," Yates told CNBC's Steve Sedgwick. "There was this inflation, which has brought out the cost-of-living protesters who would have been disgruntled at any rate."
Yates said another factor is France's 2027 presidential election, as opposition parties seek to capitalize on growing public discontent with President Emmanuel Macron .
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has proposed a 2027 budget aimed at narrowing France's deficit , projected at 5.4% of gross domestic product this year. Measures include freezing the civil service pay index and tightening reimbursement for sick leave.
"Finally there's the students, the poor students who started this by making reasonable demands for having their dilapidated infrastructure repaired and perhaps getting some air conditioners installed in the classrooms, and so these three forces have come together and created an out-of-control hurricane," Yates added.
The economic backdrop has also deteriorated. In the second quarter of 2026, France's unemployment rate rose to 8.3%, representing 2.7 million people, according to Insee, the national statistics bureau . The unemployment rate among 15- to 24-year-olds climbed to 21.6%.
Consumer prices rose 3.1% in September from a year earlier, up from 2.4% in August, according to final Insee data. Energy prices jumped 21.3%. Meanwhile, purchasing power per consumption unit is projected to fall 0.7% in 2026, according to Insee figures, cited by Le Monde .
Calculations by the French Institute of Economics for Le Monde estimate that the decline in purchasing power since 2024 is equivalent to a loss of 1,200 euros ($1,345) a year for a household with two adults and two children, and 600 euros for a single adult.
Portugal's Sarmento said that the situation across Europe varies, with Portugal in a stronger fiscal position and with much less debt than France.
"Those countries [those with higher public debt] have much less fiscal margin to act, but the main issue is that we need to resolve the problem of productivity and competitiveness at the European level," he said.
"The European economy is not growing as much as the U.S., and without economic growth, it's impossible to have better salaries and to have the resources for better public services and social support," Sarmento added.
In the second quarter of 2026, Portugal recorded the EU's highest annual increase in house prices, up 16.5% from a year earlier, according to Eurostat .
The Portuguese government is looking to increase the supply of housing to reduce buying and renting costs to resolve the issue, according to Sarmento.
French government bond yields rose and the euro weakened on Monday as the unrest added to investor concerns over France's debt and budget.
"It will be difficult to see the budget deficit come down without painful measures," Sharon Bell, senior European equity strategist at Goldman Sachs, told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Monday.
"Taxes could well go up for French businesses. I think taxes may generally go up in France. Fiscal consolidation means you need to either spend less or tax more. Those things are very tricky."
Mike Bell, head of market strategy at RBC BlueBay Asset Management, said France faced a "very real risk" of a sovereign debt crisis.
"What's needed in France is to get the fiscal position in order; they need to raise the retirement age — you can't retire at 62 if the average person's living to 84 — but if this is going on even before they start talking about that, then imagine what would happen on the streets of France if you tried to raise the retirement age... I mean, here in the U.K. it's 68," Bell added.

articles.title_orig: Google Cloud says a 'power event' caused today's outage
articles.title_zh: Google Cloud says a 'power event' caused today's outage
articles.content_orig:
Fells London zone, taking banks, parcel firm and property sites with it – and recovery is 'tentatively' due by 1300 UTC
Google Cloud has blamed a “power event” for taking down multiple online products for customers in Western Europe, and is pledging to restore normal service within the hour.
The unplanned downtime for customers began at 0608 UTC when europe-west-2-b, one of three local availability zones in the London region, started playing up.
According to an update on its status page , Google Cloud said at 1158 UTC that full recovery workloads should be “completed, tentatively” by 1300 UTC. Customers can expect another update at that point, with Google either giving the thumbs up, thumbs sideways or having to admit engineers are still working on a fix.
Services that went AWOL included BigQuery Data TransferService, Cloud Filestore, Cloud Run, Google App Engine, Google Cloud NetApp Volumes, Google Kubernetes Engine, and Managed Service for Apache Kafka.
So what caused online services to melt at customers including Lloyds Bank, HSBC, Royal Mail, Rightmove, DPD, BT, Cloudflare, Screwfix and Revolut? Power.
"A power event caused an outage within europe-west2-b zone. The power event is mitigated. We are seeing the recovery of services and are prioritizing the recovery of existing workloads.Customers may not be able to yet create new workloads."
The Register has asked Google for further elucidation but it said the only information is available on the status page.
The "fragility" of the cloud model is again on display, Dr Amro Al-Said Ahmad , a lecturer in computer science at Keele University told The Register . He estimates that a total of 38 services were down and out for the count.
"The incident highlights the dependency effect of modern cloud ecosystems. When a core cloud region experiences failures, the impact extends far beyond the directly affected services. Applications, APIs, databases, authentication systems, payment platforms, analytics pipelines, and third-party SaaS products that depend on those services can all experience cascading failures."
"A problem in a single cloud region can therefore propagate through an entire digital supply chain, affecting organisations that are several layers removed from the original outage. While this is a regional outage centered on europe-west2, the breadth of affected services highlights a key cloud engineering lesson: resilience is not achieved by simply moving to the cloud. True resilience requires designing for regional failures through multi-region deployments, workload portability, and tested disaster recovery procedures." ®

articles.title_orig: Data center stocks slide as Korea IPO plunges 30%, pressuring tech sentiment
articles.title_zh: Data center stocks slide as Korea IPO plunges 30%, pressuring tech sentiment
articles.content_orig:
Data center stocks struggled Tuesday following a lackluster initial public offering overnight from a South Korean cloud company that has been compared to U.S. neocloud CoreWeave.
Shares of Elice dropped 30% during their market debut overnight, as investors grow increasingly wary of artificial intelligence-dedicated computing power providers amid concerns about overcapacity.
The bearish sentiment spilled into U.S. tech equities. CoreWeave shares lost 4% just after market open Tuesday; Nebius shed about 4%. Iren was down about 6%.
HSBC said in a Monday note that the troubles for the heavily levered CoreWeave are not going away.
"Debt market woes and moderating LLM revenues are exacerbating structural concerns for neoclouds ," HSBC analyst Abhishek Shukla wrote. Shukla has a reduce rating on CoreWeave with a price target of $39, implying 36.5% downside.
Elice's IPO was small, having raised just $150 million, according to Reuters . Its market cap also equates to roughly $1.3 billion. The company provides a range of AI-related services, including cloud computing equipment, training libraries and application interfaces for businesses.
Despite its size, investors are likely looking at it as a a signal of investor sentiment toward the AI build-out.
Trouble for neoclouds, which some investors see as the weakest link in the emerging AI value chain, started earlier this month with less-than-stellar revenues reported by the private AI algorithm companies and pressure from higher interest rates.
Frontier model Anthropic showed a deceleration in quarterly revenues, with sales dropping from 140% growth in the second quarter to 45% in the third. OpenAI also disappointed, reporting revenue that was $20 billion shy of what analysts expected, analyst Stephanie Roth at Wolfe said in a Sunday note.
Profitability concerns for AI algorithm companies were the focus of a report last week from advisory firm Gartner predicting that 80% of neoclouds could cease independent operations by 2030.
"Our research indicates that enterprise and consumer AI revenue will be insufficient to support profitable returns on all planned AI capital expenditures" between 2027 and 2030, Will Sommer, senior director analyst at Gartner, said.
Gartner stood by its analysis in a Monday interview with CNBC.
"At the moment, we have more compute capacity than we have demand, and we have a lot of the tokens and processing power being given away in freemium solutions," Gartner chief forecaster John Lovelock told CNBC. "Everyone in the AI race is running for a last-man standing position. Pretty much every market that Gartner is tracking in our AI race is likely to collapse down to a duopoly."
Chip stocks are also feeling some pain on Tuesday. Micron is down close to 2% as of market open; AMD is down about 1.5%; and Nvidia is down about 1%.

articles.title_orig: UK to deploy fighter jets to defend Saudi cities from Houthi attacks
articles.title_zh: UK to deploy fighter jets to defend Saudi cities from Houthi attacks
articles.content_orig:
The U.K. said it would provide defensive military support, including fighter jets, to support Saudi Arabia as attacks by Iran-backed Houthi rebels escalate.
The Houthis, a Yemeni militant group, have launched a series of strikes on Saudi targets in recent weeks. Airport attacks in the capital city of Riyadh led to multiple fatalities, flight cancellations and property damage, while facilities belonging to oil giant Saudi Aramco were targeted last week.
"The continuing attacks from the Houthis on our ally Saudi Arabia are absolutely despicable. The targeting of the airport in Riyadh in particular shows the lengths the Houthis are going to escalate the situation in the region," U.K. Defense Secretary Wes Streeting said in a statement on Tuesday.
He added that Royal Air Force Typhoon fighter jets will fly defensive air missions to help protect Saudi airspace from drones and missiles.
"This builds on the UK equipment and personnel we already have in the country to defend against Houthi air attacks," Streeting said.
The U.K. Ministry of Defence also said that the fighter jets would operate only in a defensive role and would not conduct offensive strikes against the Houthis.
It said the Royal Air Force would also provide an Airbus A400M Atlas jet "to support the movement of defence materiel within Saudi Arabia," while U.K. military advisers will also give support to Saudi staff officers.
"Escalating violence in the Gulf can have a serious impact at home in the UK — driving up the cost of living, disrupting energy supplies and costs to British businesses. It is also causing devastation to the civilian population in Yemen," the MoD said.
"We unequivocally condemn the Houthi attacks on civilian targets like King Khalid International Airport and are clear that Saudi Arabia and the Republic of Yemen have the right to defend themselves."
Yemen's civil war has returned to full-scale fighting between the Houthis and the country's internationally recognized government amid a wider regional escalation linked to the U.S.-Iran war.
Al Jazeera reported Monday that at least 53 people were killed when the Houthis launched three ballistic missiles at a military camp in southern Yemen. CNBC was not able to independently verify the reports.

articles.title_orig: Iran regime under pressure as rebel groups escalate attacks in volatile southeast
articles.title_zh: Iran regime under pressure as rebel groups escalate attacks in volatile southeast
articles.content_orig:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu outlines his vision for the future of Iran’s Islamic regime on ‘Life, Liberty & Levin.’
A new coalition of Iranian opposition groups in the restive southeastern provinces of Sistan and Baluchistan and Kerman in the Islamic Republic have launched a string of armed attacks against the clerical regime in the region.
The six strikes claimed by the coalition known as the People’s Fighters Front (JMM) have contributed to instability in the provinces, raising pressing questions about whether armed resistance against the clerical regime in Tehran will spread and if the regime can retain control over Sistan and Baluchistan, which is a majority Iranian Sunni province.
Iran is largely a Shiite Muslim country, and the minority Iranian Sunni population has faced discrimination over the decades. Sistan and Baluchistan is the second largest of the 31 Iranian provinces.
MOJTABA KHAMENEI DEFIES ‘MALICIOUS’ ATTACKS AS US ARMY ZEROES IN ON IRAN’S 350,000 TROOPS
Sistan and Baluchistan, Iran. (Mohammad /Middle East Images/AFP via Getty Images)
Mardo Soghom, an Iran expert who has written extensively about the Islamic Republic, told Fox News Digital, "The Sunni unrest can stretch the regime's military and internal security capabilities and have a psychological impact on its forces, in addition to what they experienced during the 40-day operation by the U.S. and Israel . The armed groups would not be able to establish control of the south-east, but they can seriously weaken the regime's control."
He added, "Whether these forces are receiving assistance from the Islamic Republic's adversaries — being that the Gulf Arab states or even Israel and the U.S. — remains an open question."
Protesters and members of Iranian paramilitary Basij forces march next to the fourth generation Khorramshahr ballistic missile Khaibar displayed during an anti-Israeli rally to show their solidarity with Palestinians in Tehran on Nov. 24, 2023. (Photo by Hossein Beris/Middle East Images/AFP via Getty Images)
According to an October Human Rights Activist News Agency (HRANA) report , "The pace of violence accelerated significantly in recent weeks [in the provinces] with 18 incidents recorded in just the final 18 days of the reporting period, surpassing the total for any previous full month."
JMM coalesced as an opposition coalition in Dec. 2025 through an amalgam of Baloch nationalist organizations with the militant Sunni group Jaish al-Adl.
HRANA documented "at least 63 armed incidents were recorded across Iran’s southeastern provinces of Sistan and Baluchistan and Kerman between March 31 and Oct.10, 2026, amid a sharp escalation in armed violence in the region."
The armed resistance resulted in "at least 94 people dead and 33 injured, while official sources reported 87 fatalities and 10 injuries."
IRAN INSTALLS NEW WAR CHIEFS AS TEHRAN SIGNALS ‘PROLONGED CONFRONTATION,’ EXPERT WARNS
A woman member of the Basij paramilitary, affiliated with Iran's Revolutionary Guard, holds a machine gun on a pickup truck during a parade of pro-government Iranian women. (Sobhan Farajvan/Pacific Press/LightRocket via Getty Images)
The Baloch coalition stunned the regime on Oct. 14 with the assassinations of women members of the Basij paramilitaries, including a commander and a police officer in Sistan and Baluchistan Province. The Basij has been designated a terrorist entity by the U.S. government because it falls under the American-classified terrorist movement Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).
Just days before the attack on the female Basij commander, Iranian regime-controlled media reported that Nosrat Eftekhari, deputy for Cultural and Social Affairs of the Provincial Law Enforcement Command, was killed by a roadside bomb in Zahedan, Sistan and Baluchistan provinces.
Jason Brodsky, policy director at United Against Nuclear Iran (UANI), told Fox News Digital that "There have been periodic cycles of unrest in Sistan and Baluchistan Province over the years. What we are now witnessing is an uptick in such activity. The current commander of the IRGC’s Ground Forces, Mohammad Karami used to be governor of the province and commanded IRGC forces there. His experience in the province was one of the reasons Karami was elevated to the post in 2025 given the sensitive security situation in the country."
Brodsky continued that "I don’t see any imminent threat in terms of such a seizure of control, but a red line for Iranians, especially in the opposition, is preserving the territorial integrity of Iran. That needs to be understood in Western capitals."
MOTORCYCLE PATROLS SWARM IRANIAN CITIES, CHECKPOINTS RISE AS REGIME BRACES FOR UNREST
The Artesh, Iran's regular military, is separate from the IRGC and its affiliated Basij militia. Its forces operate across four branches: the ground forces, navy, air force and air defense force. (Photo by Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
Khalilullah Balochi, who is a Baluch activist and journalist, told Iran International that "The activities of these groups are not new; what is new is the intensification of attacks."
JMM’s devastating attacks targeting the brutal Iranian regime have generated attention from Iranian dissidents and experts.
Navid Mohebbi, who worked as a Persian media analyst for the State Department's Public Affairs Bureau, told Fox News Digital "The newly formed popular Fighters Front has carried out a series of relatively successful attacks against mid-level regime officials and security personnel in Sistan and Baluchistan province in recent months, drawing a degree of public attention. At a time when the regime is executing protesters on a daily basis, the killing of certain mid-ranking security and military operatives has been met with some satisfaction among segments of Iranian society."
He warned, however, that "Nevertheless, the Iranian public remains deeply cautious and largely distrustful of such groups. Two major concerns underpin this distrust: the possibility of separatist ambitions and the influence of radical Islamism, which is fundamentally at odds with the increasingly secular outlook of Iranian society."
AFTER 6 MONTHS OF WAR, US MUST PREPARE FOR A FUTURE AFTER IRAN’S GOVERNMENT FALLS
Iranians gather while blocking a street during a protest in Tehran, Iran on Jan. 9, 2026. (MAHSA/Middle East Images/AFP via Getty Images)
Mohebbi sees encouraging signs from the JMM, including "the coalition’s recent statements, unlike the rhetoric traditionally associated with similar groups, contain no explicit references to Baluch separatism. Instead, the coalition has identified its primary objective as dismantling the system of Velayat-e Faqih (Guardianship of the Islamic Jurist) and liberating the country from its oppression. It has explicitly declared that it seeks ‘an Iran for all Iranians."’
He continued that "The reality is that these groups lack the capacity to confront the regime in conventional warfare . Through guerrilla operations, however, they can inflict significant psychological blows on the regime and its security establishment. Whether their activities can gain traction beyond Sistan and Baluchistan will depend largely on their ability to sustain what appears to be an effort to earn broader public trust."
Beni Sabti, an Iran expert at the Institute for National Security Studies (INSS) in Israel, told Fox News Digital the coalition has "a lot of guns" and created an "armed rebellion" against the Iranian regime in the provinces. He said, however, the armed upheaval is limited to the region Baluchistan.
Sabti, who was born in Tehran, said the clerical regime in the capital Tehran does not exercise solid control over the provinces, which resembles parts of South America where some governments lost sovereignty to militias.

articles.title_orig: North Korea publishes photos of Kim Jong Un - why do rumours of his death keep coming back?
articles.title_zh: North Korea publishes photos of Kim Jong Un - why do rumours of his death keep coming back?
articles.content_orig:
Kim Jong Un has appeared in North Korean state media looking remarkably healthy for a man rumoured to have died from a brain haemorrhage.
Photographs published by state newspaper Rodong Sinmun show the 42-year-old dictator touring what the paper said was a clothing and footwear exhibition with his daughter.
The images emerged hours after a Chinese dissident who lives in the US claimed, without evidence, that Kim had been taken to a hospital in Beijing in a coma and had died.
For those who watch North Korea closely, this kind of rumour has become almost routine.
In one of the world's most secretive states, facts are often difficult to verify, creating fertile ground for speculation.
This latest claim originated with Wanjun Xie, who identifies himself as chairman of the Chinese Democratic Party, a group banned by Chinese authorities. He has previously circulated unverified claims, including speculation about the death of Chinese leader Xi Jinping.
Xie alleged that Kim suffered a severe brain haemorrhage and was transferred to Beijing because North Korea lacked the medical facilities to treat him.
He claimed Kim later died and that his body had been secretly returned to North Korea, with the regime concealing his death.
Yet the photographs tell a different story.
Kim is seen examining displays, accompanied by Kim Ju Ae and his usual entourage of officials.
While there is no way to know exactly when the images were taken, there are other reasons to doubt the claim.
There would probably be signs beyond North Korea's borders if there were a sudden collapse in Kim's health.
China could tighten security along its frontier to prepare for potential instability or refugee flows. Activity around North Korean diplomatic missions might also increase. Defectors in South Korea often receive information through informal networks along the Chinese border. None of this has happened.
South Korean intelligence officials, meanwhile, told Yonhap they had heard nothing to support the reports.
The rumour also echoes previous false alarms.
In 2020, a high-profile North Korean defector claimed he was "99% certain" Kim had died following cardiovascular surgery. Not long afterwards, Kim appeared in public and the claim unravelled.
So why do these rumours keep resurfacing? The first reason is succession.
North Korea has been ruled by the Kim family for three generations, but what happens after Kim Jong Un remains less certain than it was for his predecessors.
Kim Il Sung spent decades preparing his son, Kim Jong Il, for power. By the time Kim Il Sung died in 1994, the succession plan was firmly established. Kim Jong Il's transition was relatively smooth.
Kim Jong Un's rise was faster and more precarious. After Kim Jong Il suffered a stroke in 2008, his youngest son was rapidly promoted through the ranks. By the time his father died in 2011, he had been publicly identified as the future leader.
Even so, Kim Jong Un spent years consolidating power, purging rivals and eliminating perceived threats.
Today, South Korea's intelligence agency believes he may be preparing his daughter as a successor. She has increasingly appeared at high-profile events and military displays.
But she is thought to be only 13 years old. North Korea has never been led by a woman, and she has not been formally designated as heir. Her youth would also leave her vulnerable in any power struggle.
All of this uncertainty helps explain why rumours about Kim's health attract so much attention.
The second reason is that the rumours are not entirely implausible.
Kim is overweight and a heavy smoker. South Korea's National Intelligence Service has repeatedly warned that his lifestyle puts him at higher risk of cardiovascular disease. Heart problems and strokes also run in the Kim family.
If anything were to happen to Kim, the stakes are high for neighbouring countries and the wider international community. Any sudden leadership crisis raises difficult questions about control of North Korea's nuclear weapons and the prospect of political instability.
Would a power struggle tempt hardliners to act aggressively? Could unrest trigger a refugee crisis along the Chinese border? These are questions that concern not only Beijing and Seoul but also Washington, which maintains around 28,000 troops in South Korea.
Intelligence agencies watch Kim Jong Un closely so they are prepared for any news.
Because North Korea remains an information black hole, it is also an easy target for false reports. Only a tiny circle has regular access to its leader. Even intelligence agencies struggle to obtain reliable information, and much of what emerges is heavily caveated as unverified or highly likely rather than confirmed fact.
The regime itself is also suspected of deliberately encouraging confusion, leaking misleading information to obscure what is really happening inside the country.
So it is hard to believe that Wanjun Xie had somehow stumbled across such significant news, when it had eluded those whose job it is to stay across it.
He may simply have been seeking attention. Or he may have wanted to embarrass Beijing by highlighting its ties to Pyongyang, although those are well-established for the world to see.
Whatever his motive, Xie is far from the first person to exploit the uncertainty surrounding North Korea's leadership.

articles.title_orig: Portuguese police clear housing protest camps, arresting 55
articles.title_zh: Portuguese police clear housing protest camps, arresting 55
articles.content_orig:
Hundreds at Lisbon tent camp demand action, as Giorgia Meloni says march in Italy was exploited by ‘hooligans’
The angry protests that have convulsed Spain and France in recent weeks have spilled over to Italy and Portugal , with rioters clashing with police and setting property on fire in Milan, and a tent encampment springing up in Lisbon over the weekend.
A march in central Milan on Saturday to protest against rising living costs began peacefully but ended with masked rioters throwing stones, paving blocks and other objects at riot police and setting fire to barricades made from bar tables.
Police used water cannon and teargas to disperse the crowds, and images of the aftermath showed a severely damaged carabinieri car.
At least two police officers were injured and about 50 demonstrators, including many minors, were detained, the LaPresse news agency reported.
Italy’s prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, said that while demonstrating was a right, “setting our cities ablaze is not”. In a social media post, she said “hooligans” had exploited the protests “to sow chaos, attack those responsible for ensuring security and to hold entire cities hostage”.
Milan’s centre-left mayor, Giuseppe Sala, said that while “the reasons for the protests were understandable, the violence against law enforcement and serious damage to the city are not justifiable”.
In Lisbon, a tent camp reminiscent of the one established in Madrid three weeks ago was set up by protesters demanding action to tackle the housing crisis and living costs.
Hundreds of protesters rallied at night in Rossio Square – located in the bustling, touristic heart of the Portuguese capital – after a march that had drawn thousands of people nationwide.
The attenders vowed to stay overnight, with hundreds singing songs as they sat around the statue of King Pedro IV that dominates the square.
“The Portuguese social class that pays taxes, that which keeps this country going, is under attack and is losing its rights, notably its right to housing,” said Elena Costa, a 46-year-old social assistant. “So we are all here together to try to explain that we are suffocating.”
Antonio Margado, a 52-year-old engineer, criticised the centre-right government for “a total liberalisation of rents; owners are protected more and more, while tenants who need a house are those who are protected less and less”.
Portuguese housing prices rose by 124% between 2015 and 2024, roughly twice as fast as the EU average, according to official data. The impact is especially harsh on younger people and those in Lisbon – around a quarter of Portugal’s more than 11 million inhabitants live in the capital’s greater metropolitan area.
Saturday’s camp in Lisbon amplified a housing protest that started in the northern city of Porto, where dozens of tents had already been set up.
At the earlier protest in Lisbon called by the main CGTP union, demonstrators called for better public services, pensions and wages as well as measures against soaring housing costs.
Portugal’s prime minister, Luís Montenegro, has said his government understood that people wanted to “express their outrage at what, in their view, may be omissions in public policies”. But he has warned political rivals against “importing into Portugal climates of instability and protest that, in fact, have no support in Portuguese society”, in a likely reference to violent protests in France .
after newsletter promotion
There have also been violent demonstrations in Albania this week , where demonstrators angry over university conditions and high tuition fees have demanded the resignation of the country’s prime minister, Edi Rama.
On Saturday, protesters threw rocks, molotov cocktails, metal objects and pyrotechnic devices at police, and torched cars and litter bins, using them as blazing barricades to stop police advancing.
In a sign of the escalating violence, police fired rubber bullets on the demonstrators for the first time since the protests began. The protests continued into the night, with buildings – including a court, banks and post office – set on fire or severely damaged.
The unrest follows months of anti-government protests in the Balkan nation, initially sparked by a controversial resort development linked to the family of the US president, Donald Trump.
Growing anger over soaring rents and social inequality boiled over in Spain last month after an 87-year-old woman was evicted from her home because she was unable to pay the 230% rent increase sought by the investment firm that had bought her flat.
The plight of the late María del Carmen Abascal – and the wider issue it embodied – led to street demonstrations and the creation of a protest camp in the middle of the Spanish capital , and spurred the socialist-led government to propose emergency measures to facilitate and protect access to housing. When rightwing and far-right parties voted down those measures in congress, the prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, responded by announcing a snap general election for the end of November.
In France, fury over teacher ​absences and shabby facilities in schools in the poor northern suburbs of Paris has snowballed into a nationwide movement against inequality, weak public spending and falling standards.
More than 1,200 people were arrested in France on Saturday after protesters supporting high school students clashed with police, with some demonstrations later spiralling out of control as buildings were set ablaze and shops looted.
The Associated Press and Agence France-Presse contributed to this report

articles.title_orig: US leaving oil-for-security approach, not Middle East: Envoy Tom Barrack
articles.title_zh: US leaving oil-for-security approach, not Middle East: Envoy Tom Barrack
articles.content_orig:
Doha, Qatar — The United States is moving away from its traditional security-for-oil relationship with the Middle East and no longer seeks to dominate the region, senior US diplomat Tom Barrack has said.
However, it was not abandoning the Middle East, he added, speaking at the Global Security Forum in Doha on Tuesday — but rather reassessing its role, after years of attempts to reshape governments across the region.
“The US no longer wants to own,” said Barrack, who serves as US Ambassador to Turkiye and Special Envoy for Syria. “The bargain is not to control, but to not leave. We’re not leaving.”
Barrack acknowledged that regional countries were increasingly recognising the limits of US involvement.
“Everybody is saying: OK, I can’t rely on America to solve all my problems,” he said.
Barrack questioned the effectiveness of previous interventions, saying that the US had been involved in 23 regime changes across the wider Middle East.
“Every time we try and intervene, change the person or the regime, it seems to have been a mistake,” he said.
His comments come as Washington and Tehran try to negotiate an end to the US-Israeli war on Iran that has destabilised the region and disrupted global energy supplies.
Political analyst Luciano Zaccara described Barrack as probably “the most realistic of Trump’s allies” in his assessment of US involvement in the Middle East.
He told Al Jazeera that Barrack had effectively acknowledged that regime change, one of Trump’s stated objectives in the war on Iran, was unlikely to succeed.
Zaccara said Barrack’s reference to regime changes in the Middle East was an acknowledgement “that what the US has been doing in the region has not been working, regardless of which administration it was”.
According to Zaccara, Barrack had stopped just short of suggesting that Trump needed to retreat from “the maximalist demands” he had made of Iran.
Qatar says negotiations between Tehran and Washington are continuing despite growing fears of renewed fighting.
Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Majed al-Ansari, speaking separately at the Global Security Forum, said mediators were continuing to exchange messages between the warring parties, with regional partners involved in efforts to reach a deal.
“We are working between the parties, continuing our job as mediator with our partners and others in the region,” he said.
Al-Ansari said the lack of public information about the negotiations should not be interpreted as a lack of progress.
“The fact that we’re not hearing about it is a good sign that we’re doing our job properly,” he said.
The diplomatic efforts come as Iran’s seven-day proposal to end the war remains on the table, with the US yet to give its response.
The plan envisages reopening the Strait of Hormuz and resuming nuclear negotiations in exchange for US concessions, including lifting the naval blockade on Iranian ports and easing economic sanctions on Tehran.
Analyst Negar Mortazavi said the diplomatic door remained open, but negotiations were stalled over the terms and sequencing of an agreement.
“Tehran wants to end the war, but it is not prepared to surrender under military or economic pressure,” she told Al Jazeera on the sidelines of the forum in Doha.
The Strait of Hormuz remains a major flashpoint, with attacks on commercial shipping raising concerns over global energy supplies. Before the US-Israeli war on Iran, one-fifth of the world’s oil and gas supplies transited through the strait.
Mortazavi said the escalation was part of Tehran’s strategy to maintain leverage against Washington despite its military disadvantages.
“Iran’s leverage has diminished but has not disappeared,” she said. “Moving tankers is not the same as restoring safe, predictable and normal maritime traffic.”
According to Mortazavi, Tehran wants to increase the economic and political costs of the war for Trump, while signalling to future US administrations that military action against Iran carries consequences.
But she warned that continued escalation posed serious risks to Iran and the wider region.
“Ultimately, neither military escalation nor economic pressure is likely to produce Iranian capitulation,” she said.
Qatar’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson also reaffirmed Doha’s support for Riyadh in the fighting against Yemen’s Houthi armed group, saying it backed Saudi Arabia in “defending their sovereignty against this attack”.
Fighting intensified in September after the Houthis seized areas along Yemen’s Red Sea coast, including the port city of Mocha. In response, forces loyal to Yemen’s internationally recognised government launched an offensive, dubbed “Dawn of Yemen”, on October 4, backed by Saudi air strikes.
The Houthis have retaliated with missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and military installations. Strikes on Riyadh’s King Khalid international airport earlier this month killed at least 14 people and wounded hundreds.

articles.title_orig: New Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Trailer Is A Throwback To The '90s N64 Ads
articles.title_zh: New Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Trailer Is A Throwback To The '90s N64 Ads
articles.content_orig:
The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time might not be Nintendo's next Switch 2 exclusive (don't worry Nintendo Switch Sports Resort , we haven't forgotten about you), but the looming 5th November release date means that the marketing campaign is in full swing.
We're getting new trailers, shorts and TV spots all over the place at the moment, and the new 'Art thou ready?' ad shared by Nintendo UK has left us sufficiently hyped and unexpectedly reminded of the N64 original's ads back in the '90s.
The new trailer (above) doesn't feature any fresh footage, but the whole thing is extremely badass. You've got scenes from the game intercut with flaming text screens asking such questions as "Willst thou flee? Or fight?" while bombastic brass tunes blast in the background. Come on, how can that not leave you excited?
Subscribe to Nintendo Life on YouTube 853k
All of this riffs on the original release's TV trailers, let's not forget. Those employed a similarly OTT backing track (from Conan, no less), and used the same fire text flare, controversially boasting the tagline, "Willst thou get the girl? Or play like one?" — later changed to "Willst thou soar? Or willst thou suck?" for obvious reasons. We've linked one such OG trailer below, so you can see the similarities for yourself.
For a game like Ocarina of Time, it feels only fitting that Nintendo goes hard on the nostalgia for the marketing — who doesn't get a bit misty-eyed thinking about their first time playing it, eh? Only a few weeks to go before we get to dive in all over again!

articles.title_orig: One of three Jensen Huang-signed RTX Spark laptops won at NVIDIA launch event is already listed for $17,150
articles.title_zh: One of three Jensen Huang-signed RTX Spark laptops won at NVIDIA launch event is already listed for $17,150
articles.content_orig:
NVIDIA today announced the availability of NVIDIA RTX Spark ™ laptops, bringing together RTX graphics and NVIDIA’s full-stack AI platform in slim, premium Windows PCs for accelerated creation, immersive gaming and powerful local AI — rolling out from ASUS, Dell, HP, Lenovo, Microsoft and MSI.
Combining decades of NVIDIA innovation into a single superchip, RTX Spark delivers up to 128GB of unified memory and 1 petaflop of FP4 AI performance to run large language models and AI agents locally. On a single device, creators, developers and gamers can move seamlessly between their everyday workflows and emerging AI agents on the familiar Windows platform.
“RTX Spark brings the power of NVIDIA AI, RTX graphics and CUDA together with Microsoft Windows in one PC for creating, gaming and running personal AI agents,” said Jensen Huang, founder and CEO of NVIDIA. “Together with Microsoft and our PC industry partners, we’re bringing creators, developers and gamers a new generation of Windows PC, built for the work they do today and the personal AI agents they’ll work with next.”
“We’re building Windows to be the platform for hybrid intelligence, where AI can run locally when it makes sense and reach the cloud when needed,” said Yusuf Mehdi, executive vice president at Microsoft. “Windows PCs powered by RTX Spark unlock powerful new local compute for creators and developers, expanding what they can create, build and run on Windows.”
A New Beginning for Windows PCs RTX Spark brings NVIDIA’s accelerated computing platform to a new generation of portable Windows PCs.
At its foundation is a single superchip combining an NVIDIA Blackwell RTX GPU and an NVIDIA Grace CPU with up to 128GB of unified memory and up to 1 petaflop of FP4 AI performance. That shared memory allows demanding creative projects and local AI models to run simultaneously and efficiently. MediaTek collaborated with NVIDIA on the custom CPU design, contributing to its best-in-class power efficiency, performance and connectivity.
All of NVIDIA’s platform innovation comes together in RTX Spark — NVIDIA CUDA ® , DLSS, OptiX™, Reflex, G-SYNC ® , TensorRT™ and hardware-accelerated video — in a device that fits in a messenger bag. Slim, efficient designs and all-day battery life bring these capabilities wherever users create, develop and play.
From Tool to Teammate RTX Spark gives users the capabilities to deploy local AI agents that turn the PC from a tool into an everyday teammate that can complete tasks, generate assets and write code.
Users can put agents to work immediately. Guided setup and easy installers help users get started with agents, including GitHub Copilot, Hermes, OpenClaw, Perplexity, Pi and WorkBuddy, without requiring a command line.
“Personal AI becomes more useful when it can work with your tools and help get things done,” said Dillon Rolnick, CEO at Nous Research, creators of Hermes Agent. “We brought Hermes to RTX Spark so people can put open AI models and agents to work locally on a Windows laptop, with greater control over their data and the freedom to shape AI around their own workflows.”
NVIDIA’s models and tools build on that ecosystem. Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB, a 74-billion-parameter model optimized for tool calling and multistep tasks, brings more capable local AI to supported RTX Spark configurations.
The NVIDIA OpenShell ™ secure runtime and Microsoft Execution Containers help users control agent permissions, while NVIDIA agent skills let compatible agents work with tools including NVIDIA Broadcast , RTX Remix and Omniverse ™ libraries. For example, compatible agents can adjust Broadcast effects during a stream or batch-process recorded clips, all on a local PC.
That experience extends across devices with NVIDIA PAIR , letting RTX Spark serve AI inference to compatible Windows, Linux and macOS computers on a home network while keeping other PCs free for creating and gaming.
Create, Innovate, Play RTX Spark helps creators move from an idea to finished content wherever they work, with the ability to edit 8K 4:2:2 video and render large 3D scenes up to 90GB, even when unplugged.
With the arrival of RTX Spark, Adobe is enhancing its industry-leading creative applications, including Photoshop, Premiere and Substance 3D, with NVIDIA TensorRT acceleration in AI-editing features. In Premiere, creators can work faster across some of the most intensive parts of post-production, from playback and rendering to effects, color grading and more. Photoshop and Premiere offer native RTX Spark support through beta releases available at launch, with Substance coming soon.
“Creatives are pushing the boundaries of what’s possible across image, video, audio and 3D, and they need tools that can keep up with their ambitions,” said Deepa Subramaniam, vice president of product marketing for creative professionals at Adobe. “By combining NVIDIA’s advanced computing technology with Adobe’s industry-leading creative applications, we’re delivering enhanced experiences that empower creatives to bring their ideas to life with greater power and speed.”
For enhancing recorded content, NVIDIA Broadcast 2.3 lets creators remove background noise from existing recordings and shape their voice with Studio Voice Mic Profiles. Beta RTX Video features enable up to 4K super resolution and 4x frame generation.
In ComfyUI, new RTX Video nodes can turn 15 frames-per-second (fps) AI-generated video into smoother 60 fps footage and convert it to high dynamic range without requiring per-use cloud inference charges.
Code, Test and Deploy With One Machine As AI shifts software development from writing code to directing agents, work often spans a laptop, a cloud AI model and a cloud virtual machine for testing.
RTX Spark brings coding, testing and prototyping onto one machine. Native CUDA support lets developers run models and agents locally, keeping locally processed code and context on their device with a path to deploy across more than 150 million NVIDIA RTX™ AI PCs and NVIDIA GPUs in the cloud. Windows Developer Config streamlines setup, while Windows Subsystem for Linux provides familiar Linux tools used in cloud development.
NVIDIA Skills , an open source GitHub repository, teaches agents to use NVIDIA CUDA-X ™ tools and libraries, helping developers build NVIDIA-accelerated apps without CUDA expertise.
NVIDIA and Microsoft have readied developer tools for RTX Spark, including the first PyTorch-CUDA build for Windows on Arm, the first Python build that is native by default, the first native Conda installer, support for 97% of the top 15,000 Python packages, and coding agents such as GitHub Copilot and Pi.
Game Ready With Hundreds of Games RTX Spark brings immersive gaming to the same portable Windows PC used for creating and developing, with NVIDIA Blackwell RTX graphics enhancing image quality and accelerating performance in supported titles.
Launch support spans single-player adventure and online multiplayer games including Cyberpunk 2077, Fortnite, Gears of War: E-Day, Marvel Rivals, World of Warcraft and NBA 2K27 .
NBA 2K27 showcases that immersive experience, using NVIDIA DLSS 5 technology with the 3D-Guided Neural Rendering feature to enhance lighting and material details for greater realism. A new 2x faster AI model, available today, boosts DLSS 5 frame rates by up to 1.4x. NVIDIA’s suite of RTX gaming technologies — DLSS, ray tracing, G-SYNC and Reflex — bring sharper visuals, smoother gameplay and greater responsiveness.
“Bringing the energy of NBA basketball to life means making every detail feel authentic,” said Peter Kavic, senior producer for visual concepts at 2K. “We worked with NVIDIA to bring ‘NBA 2K27’ to RTX Spark, using DLSS 5 with 3D-Guided Neural Rendering to deliver richer lighting and boost the visual quality of materials to deliver a jump in photorealism on a new generation of slim laptops and compact desktops.”
