articles.title_orig: ‘We’ve never seen a 44% decline in demand for a brand’: Converse is in free fall and some suspect Nike may sell it
articles.title_zh: ‘We’ve never seen a 44% decline in demand for a brand’: Converse is in free fall and some suspect Nike may sell it
articles.content_orig:
Three years ago, Nike executives touted “strong growth” across Converse and Jordan Brand. Now, both are declining by double digits — and so is China.
When Nike veteran Elliott Hill was tapped to take on the CEO role two years ago, the headlines largely revolved around a DTC strategy that had gone too far, leaving wholesale partners feeling abandoned and allowing competitors a chance to gain a stronger foothold at retail.
Also at issue was an overly generous distribution strategy that flooded the market with some of Nike’s core footwear franchises — namely the Air Force 1, Air Jordan and Dunk — denting their cool factor.
At the time, Hill had a simple answer to these problems : “Let’s see more of Nike being Nike.” A turnaround required the sportswear giant to refocus its organization on sport, accelerate product innovation, reset its core footwear franchises and reignite its relationship with wholesale partners.
The company — which had already cut about 2% of its workforce earlier that year — announced additional layoffs in 2025, this time amounting to less than 1% of its workforce , as Hill restructured the company around key sports versus consumer demographics. These cuts would set Nike “up to win,” a spokesperson said at the time.
Except that wasn’t the end of it either. Nike’s latest earnings report included another operational reset , which calls for an unspecified number of layoffs in the new year. And Nike’s problems have now grown to include more than just DTC and some oversupplied franchises.
John Donahoe, who led the retailer’s ill-fated DTC push, at the end of fiscal 2023 touted “strong growth” across Nike, Jordan and Converse . He said the consumer was “back” in China and that Jordan was “well on its way to becoming the second largest footwear brand in North America.”
Three years later, Converse, China and the Jordan brand are all declining in the double digits . So is sportswear, which contains some of the brand’s main footwear franchises.
“Taken together, Sportswear, Jordan Brand and Greater China represent significant work ahead,” Hill said on the company’s latest earnings call , “but we know what healthy looks like and we're taking deliberate actions to get there.”
While declines at Converse are concerning in their own right, we look below at the three areas Hill identified as critical for improvement as Nike embarks on its latest restructuring plan.
Nike’s sportswear segment, which includes some of its largest footwear franchises, was down low double-digits in the retailer’s most recent quarter. It represented a little under half of the retailer’s revenue in the quarter.
“The decline reflected a combination of deliberate actions, product underperformance and broader marketplace pressure,” Hill said.
One of those deliberate actions was the reduction of Dunk revenue by almost 50%, which excised $200 million from the division’s top-line in Q1. Some older footwear within the sportswear segment also sold “below expectations,” Hill said. Future order books are taking a hit as well, as Nike works with wholesale partners to move through excess inventory.
“In the sportswear category in particular the company feels out of touch. At this point we are questioning whether Elliott Hill may be over his head when it comes to this category and how it needs to be approached,” Jessica Ramírez, co-founder and managing director of The Consumer Collective, said in emailed comments at the time. “At this rate we believe competitive sportswear brands and lifestyle brands with strong sneaker assortments — and that are growing their lifestyle offerings and image — will further dent Nike's market share.”
There are some bright spots, including a new Studio Fleece launch , which was the retailer’s best-performing apparel collection during the quarter. The Air Force 1 is also now “driving a stable full-price business,” Hill said, and other footwear franchises grew by double digits in the quarter.
“Where we have introduced newness at scale, we've seen early success,” he added.
Still, problems in the category will likely continue to hurt Nike’s sales through its current fiscal year and into the next one.
“Overall, there's a lack of energy in the lifestyle space right now, which is impacting traffic,” Hill said. “Yes, the consumer is cautious. But as the leader in the industry, it's on us to bring more creativity to sportswear.”
After facing revenue declines in both fiscal 2025 and fiscal 2026, Greater China kicked off Nike’s fiscal 2027 with another 22% decline.
Nike has a couple of plans in place to restore the region to growth. New leadership was announced in January, with longtime Nike veteran Cathy Sparks taking on oversight of the geography as vice president and general manager of Greater China. The leaders of Nike’s four regions also joined Hill’s senior leadership team as of December.
Nike announced over the summer a plan to reset its online distribution model in China as well, which had become overly fragmented. The brand is sold across more than 1,000 digital storefronts, many of which are run by just 16 Nike partners. Come January, Nike will sell through the Nike app and website in China, and on Nike flagship experiences on Tmall, JD.com and Douyin.
The effort is aimed at creating “a more premium brand presentation with clearer product stories and a more connected consumer journey,” Hill said in early October.
Nike will also invest in local product creation in China, with the first collection made specifically for the Chinese consumer launching this month.
“It will be a brick-and-mortar only launch purposely,” Hill said. “And then we will continue to deliver products over time, products and assortments that are locally designed, developed and even manufactured in China.”
The retailer has its eye on the brick-and-mortar experience more broadly in China, noting that many of its partners have not refreshed their stores over the past seven years.
“In the near term, revenues and profitability in China will be impacted,” Hill said. “We expect our digital cleanup to take multiple seasons as we continue to take targeted actions with our partners to improve inventory levels.”
As a result, declines in Greater China will be “even worse the remainder of the year,” Needham analysts led by Tom Nikic said in emailed comments. Like sportswear, China is likely to be impacting Nike well into fiscal 2028, Nikic noted.
Muddying the waters is a plan to consolidate Nike’s four geographies into three: As part of the Pace restructuring program, Greater China will join a larger group in fiscal 2028 that also contains Asia Pacific. BNP Paribas Equity Research analyst Laurent Vasilescu noted that this will give analysts less visibility into trends in China, which is “critically important” to understanding Nike’s future growth.
“While this change has already been known, we believe it is unfairly being done under the guise of restructuring when it is simply a way for Nike to create a new APGC (Asia Pacific and Greater China) segment and give investors less transparency in disaggregating China sales,” Vasilescu wrote.
At the same time, Vasilescu noted that Nike has stopped reporting comparable store sales by region, something it has done since fiscal year 2011.
“Not only does the pulling of this disclosure make years of comp store sales data not useful for comparisons sake, but it reduces the transparency on if brick and mortar growth is being driven by like for like sales or simply unit expansion,” Vasilescu wrote.
The Jordan Brand, which raked in $8.7 billion in fiscal 2024, was down roughly 20% from that benchmark by the end of fiscal 2026. In Q1, revenue fell again, this time by the mid-teens.
Jordan made up about 13% of Nike’s business in the quarter, according to Hill. The issue, the executive said, is that Nike has been oversupplying its retro Jordan product.

articles.title_orig: What if an AI bubble bursts — and that accelerates AI job losses? : Planet Money
articles.title_zh: What if an AI bubble bursts — and that accelerates AI job losses? : Planet Money
articles.content_orig:
This article first appeared in the Planet Money newsletter. You can sign up here .
What if an AI bubble bursts, triggering a recession, and that recession ends up accelerating the replacement of workers with AI? Call it the AI double whammy.
I've long been skeptical of sweeping claims about how AI will transform the world. I still am. We don't really know. But as this technology advances, I've found myself worrying more about what it could mean for our livelihoods.
Two strands of economic research have given me reason to take this double whammy seriously. One concerns the history of financial bubbles. The other concerns a surprising relationship between recessions and automation, when businesses use technology to do tasks that were previously done by humans.
First, the bubbles. In 1978, the economist Charles Kindleberger published an influential book titled Manias, Panics, and Crashes: A History of Financial Crises . Drawing on the theoretical work of economist Hyman Minsky, Kindleberger went through centuries of economic history and saw a recurring pattern.
Often the bubble starts with some big potential change to the economy. A revolutionary new technology, for example, that promises to transform industries and create enormous wealth. Investors have a good reason to be excited by it. But they get overly excited. During the upswing, they bet tons of money expecting basically that the sky is the limit. And they often build up debt in the process, borrowing money to make even bigger bets and thereby helping to further fuel the boom. That debt can become a ticking time bomb. When reality sets in, asset prices fall, but those debts remain. Borrowers struggle to repay, lenders suffer losses, and a market crash can spiral into a financial crisis and a painful recession.
One crucial insight is that a technology can truly be revolutionary, yet still fuel a bubble that ends in a financial crash. For example, the railroads. I wrote about that bubble in a previous Planet Money newsletter — and how its collapse triggered "The Panic of 1873." The ensuing economic turmoil helped foment a populist uprising and the first major immigration crackdown in American history.
AI is now basically propping up the U.S. stock market. An analysis from J.P. Morgan earlier this month found that just 42 AI-related companies accounted for around two-thirds of the S&P 500's stock price gains since early 2024. Meanwhile, AI-related companies are borrowing hundreds of billions of dollars to help finance data centers and the energy infrastructure to power them.
None of this proves that what we're witnessing is a bubble or that this debt is a ticking time bomb for the financial system. The bursting of the dot-com bubble helped usher in a relatively mild recession. Debt played a smaller role in that boom, helping to limit the financial fallout. Its collapse did not trigger a systemic financial crisis like the one that followed the housing market bust around 2008.
Even without a financial crisis, though, there could be a painful reckoning. Will all these companies ultimately make enough money to justify all their borrowing and spending? Will each company survive? Technology analyst Benedict Evans has warned that fierce competition between companies offering similarly capable AI models could drive down the prices they can charge and leave little room for profit — even as they're spending ungodly amounts of money to develop and run these models.
If an AI bust triggers a recession, that would be painful enough. But this is where a few studies add to my anxieties. Because they suggest that recessions can be the very moment when businesses turn to new technologies to replace workers.
We tend to imagine automation as a gradual process. Technology improves, businesses adopt it, and jobs slowly change or disappear, theoretically while new jobs appear in other parts of the economy. But this research suggests that automation can happen in bursts, and those bursts tend to cluster around recessions.
One study , by economists Nir Jaimovich and Henry Siu, found that jobs vulnerable to previous waves of automation saw most of their decline around recessions. Between 1990 and 2017, 88% of the decline in the share of Americans employed in these jobs occurred during recessions or in the months immediately before or after them.
And here's the unsettling irony: fierce price competition could keep AI companies from delivering the profits investors expect, while making their technology cheaper for other businesses to use to replace workers. If an AI bust triggers a recession, that downturn could accelerate worker replacement. Investors could lose their money, and workers could still lose their jobs.
It's a nightmare scenario. First, the bust hammers our retirement savings. Then, as businesses scramble to cut costs, many of our jobs are permanently lost.
Of course, we still don't know whether AI will deliver enough profits to justify all the borrowing and spending, whether a bust would trigger a painful recession, or whether the automation patterns found in past recessions will repeat themselves with AI. A downturn could leave businesses with less money to invest in AI. And AI could still prove more useful for helping workers get more productive than outright replacing them.
Whether AI delivers one whammy or two whammies or none, there are policies that can limit the damage when workers lose their jobs. Obviously, unemployment insurance and other policies like that. And people like Bill Gates are proposing that we should tax AI and robots , making it more economical to continue employing humans while generating revenue that the government can spend to enhance the safety net. That idea is something we might explore in a future newsletter.
So, yeah, there are reasons this nightmare might never come true, and there are ways to limit the damage if it does. That, however, hasn't stopped me from worrying about it.
But it felt cathartic writing this down — getting these worries out of my head and onto the page.

It will feature Daron Acemoglu, a Nobel Prize-winning professor at MIT who's been critical of AI companies, and Ronnie Chatterji, a professor at Duke and chief economist at OpenAI. articles.title_orig: I’ve used the Pixel 11 Pro XL and iPhone 18 Pro Max, and Apple’s ecosystem isn’t enough anymore
articles.title_zh: I’ve used the Pixel 11 Pro XL and iPhone 18 Pro Max, and Apple’s ecosystem isn’t enough anymore
articles.content_orig:
Google unveiled the Pixel 11 series in mid-August 2026, but the new phones have been met with a somewhat lackluster response from early reviewers, especially the base Pixel 11 model. Plenty of good Pixel 11 alternatives exist in the rich Android ecosystem, but consumers who are loyal to Google phones may not want a Galaxy or Moto phone. These buyers have a different option to upgrading this year, particularly if they own a Pixel 9 or Pixel 10 model: They can wait for the Pixel 12 (or later), and keep using their current devices. They may want to consider a battery replacement, but only if the battery health has dropped below 80%.
Using a 2024 or 2025 Pixel phone instead of buying the newest model makes even more sense in the current landscape. Smartphone vendors have been forced to increase prices in response to the AI-related mobile RAM crisis. Google is no different, with the cheapest Pixel 11 starting at $899, $100 more than the Pixel 9 and Pixel 10 . While the handset comes with 256 GB of storage instead of 128 GB, it doesn't offer that many appealing upgrades, and the Tensor G6's performance is one example. Google's newest processor is well behind competitors when it comes to raw performance. The chip isn't a match for the A20 Pro chip powering the iPhone 18 Pro handsets in benchmarks, and it can't even compete against the iPhone 17's A19. Similarly, as Tom's Guide has shown, the Tensor G6 can't outperform Qualcomm's Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 that powers the Galaxy S26.
Replacing an old Pixel battery would be significantly cheaper than buying the new phone, but a replacement may not be necessary. Many Pixel 9 and Pixel 10 users may still have batteries that are in good health.
The Pixel 11 is almost identical to its predecessors in some ways, especially if you only look at hardware specifications. It has the same 6.3-inch display (2,424-by-1,080 resolution and 60-120 Hz refresh rate). It's slightly brighter than the Pixel 9, but brightness matches the Pixel 10's screen (up to 3,000 nits). The new phone has similar measurements (6 by 2.8 by 0.3 inches). It comes with 12 GB of RAM like the previous phones but supports up to 512 GB of storage. The camera hardware is similar to the Pixel 10, featuring 48-megapixel wide, 13-megapixel ultrawide, and 10.8-megapixel telephoto shooters. The Pixel 9 has only two cameras on the back: 50-megapixel wide and 48-megapixel ultrawide. All three phones feature 10.5-megapixel selfie cameras.
The battery size is almost identical to the Pixel 10 (4,985 mAh vs. 4,970 mAh), and slightly larger than the Pixel 9's 4,700 mAh battery. Of the three phones, only the Pixel 9 doesn't support Pixelsnap (magnetic) wireless charging. The Pixel 11 also offers faster Pixelsnap charging than the Pixel 10 (25 W versus 15 W). Wired charging is similar for the three phones (30 W versus 30 W versus 27 W). Google's battery life estimate for the Pixel 11 is 30 hours, while the older phones can last for about 24 hours on a single charge.
All three handsets are rated IP68 for water and dust resistance. They feature Gorilla Glass Victus 2 screens, in-display fingerprint sensors, and USB-C ports. The Pixel 9 supports Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 5.3, and has a slot for physical SIM cards. The newer handsets come with Wi-Fi 6E, Bluetooth 6.0, and dual eSIM support. Finally, all three handsets will offer seven years of updates, including major Android releases and security patches.
Since each Pixel generation launches with exclusive, new software features, the Pixel 11 has an advantage over its predecessors in this department. It comes with Gemini Intelligence, Rambler, and Magic Capture. There's no telling when or if these features will be available on older Pixel models. But given the major hardware similarities between the three handsets, Pixel 9 and Pixel 10 owners may be better off sticking with their current devices. There is one scenario where an upgrade would make sense: when the price of buying the new handset is lower than changing the battery of the old phone after taking into account any Pixel 11 discounts and trade-in offers. Between Pixel 9 and Pixel 10 owners, it's the former who would get more from an upgrade, particularly if the costs remain low.
A genuine Pixel 9 battery kit costs $59.99 from iFixit, while the Pixel 10 battery kit is even cheaper at $49.99. Taking the phone to an authorized repair shop for battery replacement may be a better idea, but a professional installation will add labor costs. However, it's likely that many Pixel 9 and Pixel 10 phones will not need battery replacements soon.
All three phones contain batteries that are rated for 1,000 charge cycles before battery health drops below 80%. Only when that happens will a battery replacement be advised. The phone will show a warning in the Settings app under Battery Health, advising the owner that a replacement is needed. Assuming most owners go through a full charge cycle per day, the Pixel 9 would be at over 750 cycles since its August 2024 launch. The Pixel 10 would be at around 400 cycles since August 2025.

articles.title_orig: Some Google Home Speakers caught downloading hundreds of gigs of data
articles.title_zh: Some Google Home Speakers caught downloading hundreds of gigs of data
articles.content_orig:
Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...
A bug in some Google Home speakers is causing them to download large amounts of data for no clear reason. The issue doesn’t affect all Google speakers, but multiple reports from Reddit and media outlets suggest its newest speaker may be the most affected.
9to5Google found that one of its speakers had consumed 17GB of data in a 24-hour period. The timing of the downloads each day strongly suggests it may be a failed firmware update that keeps repeatedly downloading.
The largest known report comes from Reddit, where one person shared that their speaker had consumed 3.3TB of data over the last month, with most of the data downloaded in early October.
Other social media posts share similar issues, including one in which a speaker attempted to download 140GB of data overnight. Other Google Home products in the same household downloaded 81.7GB and 65.3GB, suggesting a widespread issue.
Google has yet to share what the problem is, but a spokesperson told 9to5Google, "A fix is already rolling out that should address this for users.”
To see if you’ve been impacted, look at your router’s data results and see how much your Google Home devices have been consuming. If you’re on a limited data plan with your internet service provider, this issue may mean you’re encroaching on your data allowance .
If that’s the case, consider turning off your Google Home speaker for the foreseeable future and turning it on for short periods in the coming weeks to see whether the most recent fixes have reached your device.

articles.title_orig: Live Updates: Iran lauds ties with Russia, contradicting Trump's claim of little Russian support for Tehran
articles.title_zh: Live Updates: Iran lauds ties with Russia, contradicting Trump's claim of little Russian support for Tehran
articles.content_orig:
Tehran, Iran – Russia’s Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has met his Iranian counterpart Abbas Araghchi in Tehran, to discuss the war with the United States and efforts to end it.
Lavrov landed in the Iranian capital on Monday afternoon on his first visit to Iran since February 2025.  Araghchi said talks with Lavrov had focused on regional developments, including the US-Israeli war on Iran.
He also called out Israel’s “dangerous expansion” in the region, which he blamed for the current hostilities.
“The existing insecurity around the Strait of Hormuz is a direct result of the military aggression by the US and [Israel] against Iran, and it is ongoing in different forms,” he said.
He added that Iran’s policy was to focus on diplomacy, as regional problems have “no military solution”.
“I believe Europe must also open its eyes to some truths,” Araghchi said. “Just like the Americans, the Europeans suffer from miscalculations and wrong interpretations, and have caused many wars and troubles around the world with their wrong policies.”
Meanwhile, Lavrov said Russia is committed to a 20-year strategic partnership agreement with Iran, which officially came into force on October 2. He said Russian specialists would gradually return to the Bushehr nuclear power plant after they left during the war.
The Russian foreign minister also linked restored navigation with protection for Iran against renewed attacks.
Lavrov held a meeting with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian later on Monday. Pezeshkian said that he believes Russia shared “common views and approaches with Iran” when it came to his call for a world based on mutual respect.
Moscow said Lavrov’s trip was part of efforts to ease months of tension, since the US and Israel launched their war on Iran on February 28.
On Sunday, Lavrov was in Bahrain, which was heavily targeted by Iran during the war, to participate in a strategic dialogue session between Russia and the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC).
He was urged by GCC members to use Moscow’s influence with Tehran to press for “serious dialogue” and restore shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, which has been severely disrupted by attacks on commercial vessels.
GCC chief Jasem Al-Budaiwi said member states had faced more than 7,000 Iranian missiles and drones since the start of the war.
In the council’s closing statement, the six Arab countries said they wanted Iran’s nuclear and missile programmes, as well as its support for regional armed groups, to be included in future talks to end the war.
Nikita Smagin, an analyst and researcher on Iran and Russia’s role in the Middle East, said Lavrov’s trip reflects Moscow’s efforts to maintain working relations with all countries in the region.
He said Lavrov also wants to maintain Russia’s status as a mediator, despite the impact of the Ukraine war on its global reputation.
“The timing of visits to the Gulf monarchies and Iran, taking place almost simultaneously, is a deliberate signal: Moscow wants to show that it approaches relations with all these countries on broadly equal terms and is equally interested in cooperation with each of them,” Smagin said.
Lavrov told GCC ministers in Manama that the region was once again teetering on the brink of a full-scale war and Russia wanted to establish a regional architecture for “collective security”.
He said this could include combining initiatives from countries in the region, along with those put forward by Russia and China, with the aim of restoring maritime traffic and achieving lasting peace. The Russian foreign minister urged other regional states such as Iraq and Jordan, which have also been hit by Iranian strikes, to participate.
Lavrov expressed support for the Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) signed between Iran and the US in June, which later collapsed, as a framework for reducing tension.
Iran has said it wants a return to that agreement, and for Washington to honour a finalised bilateral deal between Iran and Oman to manage territorial waters in the Strait of Hormuz. This has been opposed by the US, which has established its own route in the waterway for shipping.
Intelligence reports cited by US media said that Russia and China are providing military support to Iran in the form of satellite imagery for targeting purposes and components for weapons.
But US President Donald Trump contradicted those reports last week, saying Moscow and Beijing would have “too much to lose” if they helped Iran.
Washington has also issued sanctions waivers for Russia in a bid to lower fuel prices driven up by the war against Iran.
Russia’s position on the Iran war is somewhat unusual, said Smagin. It has a partial interest in the conflict continuing, as higher oil prices and the severe restrictions on Iranian oil reaching China all benefit Moscow.
“Russia and Iran have been competing primarily for the Chinese market, so China is now effectively forced to buy Russian oil at higher prices because Iranian supplies are largely unavailable,” he said.
Smagin added that Russia does not want the conflict to escalate further, as the consequences could be unpredictable, but its leverage over either Iran or the US to influence the course of the conflict remains limited.
Russia will continue to expand relations with Tehran, Smagin said, including through Caspian Sea trade, and limited military cooperation with Iran.
“These efforts appear to be aimed less at generating economic returns than at expanding Russia’s political influence over Iran and the course of events,” he said.
Military strikes by Iran and the US to wrest control of the waterway have continued, with the US midterm elections approaching on November 3 .
In comments to the media, Trump threatened to “soon finish the job” with Iran, to which Iranian Foreign Minister Araghchi replied: “We have unfinished jobs too.”

articles.title_orig: Lawmaker reportedly loses leg as car ramming stuns Australia
articles.title_zh: Lawmaker reportedly loses leg as car ramming stuns Australia
articles.content_orig:
An Australian lawmaker was in critical but stable condition Tuesday after being hit by a car in what authorities said was a deliberate attack, shocking a nation where political violence is extremely rare.
Helen Haines, a 65-year-old independent member of Parliament, was struck Monday by a white Toyota Land Cruiser outside her electoral district office in Wangaratta, a town of about 30,000 people in the southern Australian state of Victoria. She underwent surgery overnight after being airlifted to a hospital in the state capital of Melbourne, about 150 miles away.
Local media reported that one of Haines’ legs had been amputated and that she was fighting to keep her other leg. The Alfred Hospital in Melbourne did not respond to an NBC News request for comment on the reports.
Australian lawmaker in critical condition after car ramming
Police charged the driver, who they said was a 43-year-old local man, on Tuesday with intentionally causing serious injury, dangerous driving causing serious injury and causing harm to a federal official.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said earlier Tuesday that according to eyewitnesses, the driver had passed Haines and then did a  U-turn, hitting her as she was standing by the trunk of her parked car.
“It’s clear that there was a deliberate act here. This wasn’t an accident, someone, you know, just skidding off the road,” he told the Australian Broadcasting Corp., adding that the motivation was not yet clear.
Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke told the network that witnesses had described seeing the driver reverse and then hit Haines a second time.
The suspect’s father said the family knew Haines well.
She was a “deeply respected, valued and much loved member of our local community,” Brendan Nugent’s father, Rod Nugent, and his partner, Christine Cunningham, said in a statement Tuesday.
“Helen has been our friend for more than 20 years and what happened to her yesterday is devastating and unfathomable,” the statement added.
Political violence is extremely rare in Australia , where lawmakers are often out in public with little or no security and their accessibility is a point of national pride.
“It’s an Australian tradition to have a chat to a politician that you bump into at the shops,” Josh Roose, an associate professor of politics at Deakin University in Melbourne, told NBC News in an interview.
But threats are rising as political rhetoric becomes more extreme, officials and experts say, particularly since the Covid pandemic.
According to the Australian Federal Police, there were 1,067 incidents of threats, harassment, nuisance or offensive behavior against senior officeholders, parliamentarians and protected locations in the 2025-26 financial year, a 12% increase over the previous year and twice the number five years earlier.
In a 2023 study of Victoria state parliamentarians, 82% reported harassment and 85% reported threats of harm, said Josh Holloway, a senior lecturer in government at Flinders University in Adelaide, with female politicians more likely to face abuse.
Holloway said that Australian federal lawmakers, especially those in rural areas, typically work from “shopfront-style offices,” hold regular community meetings and attend local events without security.
Those practices may now come under scrutiny, “but reducing public access to their representatives can come with significant democratic cost,” he said in emailed comments.
Albanese said Tuesday that it was everyone’s responsibility to “turn the temperature down.”
“We can disagree with each other, but do it in a respectful way,” he told Australia’s “Today” show. “And that’s something that Helen Haines always was characterized by, was that respect that she showed to others right across the political spectrum.”
Albanese said later that he had spoken by phone with local barber Ricky Jefferies, who ran from his nearby shop to help detain Haines’ attacker in what Albanese said was “a great example of the Australian spirit.”
“I heard a loud bang, with no brakes. It was crazy,” Jefferies told reporters. “I just ran out the front to see what was happening.”
Jefferies, who said he removed a knife from the suspect’s pocket and pulled him out of the car, said a lot of people “just ran to help.”
Haines, a mother and grandmother who spent three decades working in rural health as a nurse and midwife and has a doctorate in childbirth, was first elected to Parliament in 2019, then re-elected in 2022 and 2025. Her family said in a statement that they were grateful for the “swift assistance of bystanders,” as well as first responders.
The increase in political threats in Australia follows a similar trend in the United States and other liberal democracies, Roose said.
“Australia always echoes what we’re seeing internationally, but sometimes slightly behind,” he said.
Since the pandemic, there has emerged a “level of extremist discourse that is unparalleled in Australian history,” Roose said, one that is highly influenced by politics in the U.S.
Australia, and particularly Victoria, had some of the strictest pandemic lockdowns in the world, which left residents feeling  “imprisoned, but also disempowered,” he said.
Lingering feelings of resentment combined with the current high cost of housing, fuel and other necessities have contributed to a “deep hostility” toward the government, Roose said.
Politics in rural Australia, especially, have become “highly inflammatory,” he said, “because of the online space and the poverty and the desperation that, quite frankly, has seeped into these areas.”
Roose said the “paradox” was that the victim was Haines, who is not considered a polarizing figure and is “someone who’s grown up and spent most of their life in these regions.”
“It indicates, I suppose, the challenge facing democracies around the world,” he said.
Jennifer Jett is the Asia Digital Editor for NBC News, based in Hong Kong.

articles.title_orig: Exclusive | Real-Estate Giant CBRE Gets Deeper Into Data Centers With $1 Billion Deal
articles.title_zh: Exclusive | Real-Estate Giant CBRE Gets Deeper Into Data Centers With $1 Billion Deal
articles.content_orig:
Image by Ralph from Pixabay
A UK-based datacentre infrastructure provider that builds and maintains kit for major tech firms has been snapped up for up to $1bn.
Ranking 31 st in Oxygen 250 2026 , London-based Cisco, HPE, Fortinet and Commscope partner Onnec is selling up to US-based real estate and investment services giant CBRE Group .
Built on four brands in the form of Excel, Redstone, Kedington and Load Service s , Onnec specialises in the design, deployment and maintenance of network, fibre and datacentre infrastructure.
CBRE said it “long believed” Onnec is an “excellent” fit for its strategy, saying the dal will boost its ability to support its clients’ global datacentre needs.
Onnec generated an adjusted EBITDA of £21.9m on revenue that boomed 41% to £193m in calendar 2025, its most recently filed accounts show.
But CBRE said it expects the acquired business to log £50m of core EBITDA on revenues of £370m by 2027.
“CBRE is pursuing an explicit strategy to build a global infrastructure services business to complement our real estate services business. We’ve long believed Onnec is an excellent fit in this strategy,” stated CBRE COO Vikram Kohli.
“The acquisition is also consistent with our ongoing effort to build resilient businesses that benefit from secular tailwinds.”
To land Onnec – which counts hyperscalers and global financial services firms among its clientele – CBRE is ponying up an initial £460m in cash plus a multi-year earnout of up to £300m.
Subject to customary regulatory approvals, the deal is expected to be completed around the end of the year.

articles.title_zh: As Politicians Argue About China, US Patients Find Cutting-Edge Treatment There
articles.content_orig:
Until recently, a Manhattanite might venture no more than a few dozen blocks to find the world’s most sophisticated cancer treatment. Cutting-edge American medicines have helped reduce the U.S. cancer death rate by about a third since 1990, and New York City hospitals deliver some of the best care in the country.
But in January 2025, the city’s health systems had no good options for Debbie Doppelt, a 60-year-old jeweler with an unusual form of lung cancer that mostly afflicts nonsmokers like her. The Food and Drug Administration hadn’t yet approved sunvozertinib, a drug developed in China that targets the mutation driving Doppelt’s tumors. She had been through chemotherapy and surgery, but the cancer had now spread to her brain. And she didn’t qualify for the relevant clinical trials.
Then an option emerged, in an offhand remark.
“Too bad she’s not Chinese,” a doctor told her son Max Doppelt, who had organized his mother’s care since her 2023 diagnosis. “She could go to a pharmacy in China and buy it.”
Within hours, mother and son had reached out to friends and relatives, one of whom procured a small supply of sunvozertinib from a contact living in China. A few months later, Max flew to Shanghai to get a refill.
Other patients have followed. “No organization or doctor is guiding patients to China, but word gets out,” Max said. He said he knows of at least 30 Americans who’ve made the pilgrimage to obtain the drug, which the FDA licensed in July 2025 but wasn’t yet on the U.S. market as of mid-October of this year.
Sunvozertinib, made by Shanghai-based Dizal Pharmaceutical, isn’t the only treatment drawing patients to China. Americans, Europeans, and others are trekking there to enter clinical trials for CAR-T therapy, an area in which China is now a world leader .
China, until recently known more as a supplier of drug precursor chemicals and generic medicines, has become a biotech powerhouse, accounting for as much as 46% of new drugs tested around the world in 2025. U.S. pharmaceutical companies are testing new therapies there and signing billion-dollar contracts with Chinese firms to develop and market their drugs.
China’s progress has alarmed some politicians, who warn of lost jobs and U.S. dependency on Chinese medicines. The Trump administration in June kicked off Operation TrialBlazer, aimed at speeding up some FDA regulatory processes to lure back more clinical trials.
China’s poor showing in vaccine and drug development during the covid pandemic prompted the country to overhaul its biotech sector, dramatically altering the global industry, said Sam Rasty, a veteran of small biotech companies who now leads one called FynderBio. Venture capital now flows heavily to early-stage clinical work in China and Australia, where regulatory systems enable key first-in-human studies much more quickly than in the United States.
Chinese companies are so much faster at this process that U.S. biotechs, which used to share early advances at conferences or funding meetings, now routinely conceal their progress out of fear that competitors will take their ideas and speed them to market, said Steve Potts, CEO of Breakthru Medicine, a small biotech.
At a meeting he attended in May, nearly all the 60 biotech CEOs in the room planned to run phase 1 trials in Australia, Europe, or China, Potts said. Five or 10 years ago, most of those trials would have been carried out in the U.S.
“Slow and prohibitive” FDA requirements are driving investment to more-nimble Chinese companies, President Donald Trump’s nominee to lead the agency, Heidi Overton, warned in her opening statement at her Sept. 24 confirmation hearing.
The movement of clinical trials overseas “should give pause to every American and those who serve on their behalf,” Overton said. “When we lose this advantage, we lose our health security. And when we lose our health security, we lose everything.”
Overton pledged to continue TrialBlazer, which mirrors Australian processes begun in 1991. It is aimed at accelerating clinical trials and approvals so patients do not feel compelled to seek treatment abroad, said Department of Health and Human Services spokesperson Emily Hilliard. It is sometimes legal to obtain medication abroad for personal use, but the FDA “cautions patients about potential safety and quality risks associated with treatments outside our regulatory system,” she added.
As the FDA moves to streamline drug development, members of Congress are trying to slow Chinese firms’ integration into U.S. biotech.
Rep. John Moolenaar (R-Mich.), who chairs the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, in June co-sponsored legislation with Rep. Debbie Dingell (D-Mich.) requiring all U.S. pharmaceutical deals with Chinese companies to be cleared by the Treasury Department.
Others see biotech protectionism as misguided. China’s focus on improved medicines can only help us, said Peter Kolchinsky, managing partner of RA Capital Management, which has Chinese investments in its biotech portfolio.
“We may be adversaries in many areas, but we’re not competing with them to cure cancer. We are collaborating with them to cure cancer,” he said. “There are things that are bigger enemies than any other nation on Earth.”
Subscribe to KFF Health News' free Morning Briefing.
Cancer Knows No Boundaries
A minor but persistent cough led to the diagnosis of Debbie Doppelt’s cancer in late 2023. Chemo, immunotherapy, and surgery kept it at bay for months, but in December 2024, scans showed the cancer had spread to her brain, with 10 tiny tumors.
The FDA earlier that year had approved amivantamab, a drug that targeted the mutation driving Doppelt’s tumor, but Max was concerned about its toxicity. Also, several doctors he consulted told him that amivantamab might not penetrate brain tissue to fight cancer there.
Doppelt tried to enter a clinical trial at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, where she was a patient, for zipalertinib, another drug that targeted her mutation. But in January 2025, the Doppelts learned that a slight scarring on her lungs had rendered her ineligible for the study.
That left sunvozertinib, which gained approval in China in 2023. It was also being tested in the U.S., but only in late-stage trials in which half the subjects received chemotherapy only. That risk was a nonstarter for Doppelt, whose cancer had already outsmarted chemo.
So Max flew to Shanghai, returning with 26 boxes of sunvozertinib in his luggage. The drugs cost about $10,000, he said.
“Getting on the plane and bringing the medicine home felt like my life’s purpose,” Max said. “The data was so clear that this drug had significant efficacy in the brain. Anything else she might do, she might not last a year.”
On Sept. 1 of this year, AstraZeneca signed an agreement with Dizal to distribute the drug worldwide, and it plans to make it available in the U.S. by the start of 2027, spokesperson Tara Parsell said.
Doppelt, who runs a diamond business with her husband, has tried to stay positive and healthy, scarcely missing a day of work since her 2023 diagnosis. She said she’s grateful she has a loving community and the means to afford the best available therapies.
“I think I’ve been pretty successful at having, actually, an amazing three years,” she said. “In some ways a better three years, with all of it, than the three years before, because you’re so appreciative of everything.”
Doppelt’s parents were Holocaust survivors. “They were always saying: ‘This piece of bread tastes so good! Do you know what it is to be hungry?’”
Searching for help for his mother gave Max, a 30-year-old computer engineer, an idea for helping patients find the right treatment — which, in cases of advanced cancers, may be a clinical trial.
A year ago, he quit his tech job and started a company that uses artificial intelligence to combine data from research and drug company sites with a patient’s health records to help them find the right study.

articles.title_orig: US bans govt agencies from using DeepSeek, China vows to protect firms
articles.title_zh: US bans govt agencies from using DeepSeek, China vows to protect firms
articles.content_orig:
The Trump administration banned Chinese AI startup DeepSeek from civilian U.S. government agencies, citing security concerns.
The Department of Homeland Security on Monday made public the order requiring federal civilian agencies to remove DeepSeek-related technology from their IT systems and barring them from procuring DeepSeek products and services. The ban applies to federal civilian agency IT systems, including third-party products and services developed using the company's technology.
The move comes amid intensifying geopolitical tensions between Washington and Beijing, with artificial intelligence emerging as a key battleground in the two countries' race for technological dominance.
Asked about the U.S. move by Reuters, China's foreign ministry told the news agency that it would safeguard the rights and interests of its companies.
Mao Ning, a ministry spokesperson, said that "China consistently opposes the over-generalization of national security as well as the politicization of science, technology and trade issues," the agency reported.
The order, originally issued on July 24, applies to federal civilian agencies, including the Treasury, State and Justice departments, but it excludes the Department of Defense.
Since DeepSeek burst onto the scene at the start of 2025, several U.S. government agencies have imposed various restrictions.
Congress restricted the use of DeepSeek in intelligence community systems in December 2025. Earlier that year in March, U.S. Commerce Department bureaus told staff DeepSeek was banned on government devices, Reuters reported at the time. The Defense Information Systems Agency moved to block access to DeepSeek models in January 2025, according to reports from Bloomberg.
DeepSeek's AI models "present multiple threat vectors," the latest DHS order states, citing concerns over potential access to sensitive data by Chinese authorities and potential cybersecurity vulnerabilities.
The agency also warned that using DeepSeek's AI models could result in sensitive U.S. government data being transferred to China, potentially providing intelligence on American citizens and government programs.
The models may also contain malware or other security vulnerabilities, the agency said, citing open-source research that identified multiple critical vulnerabilities in DeepSeek's iOS app.
Executive agencies can request exceptions to the order, including delays in compliance, by submitting a written justification to the DHS within 60 days of the order's issuance.
DeepSeek and China's Embassy in the U.K. did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment.

articles.title_orig: China warns UK of ‘firm countermeasures’ if it joins EU import curbs on EVs
articles.title_zh: China warns UK of ‘firm countermeasures’ if it joins EU import curbs on EVs
articles.content_orig:
Beijing warns against ‘discriminatory’ step after France drops opposition to British role in Made in Europe package
No 10 has left the door open to imposing tariffs on Chinese-made electric vehicles as part of the Made in Europe package, prompting a warning from Beijing that such a move would be “discriminatory”.
Downing Street said on Friday that it would “welcome the objective to have the UK included in the Industrial Accelerator Act” after France dropped its opposition to Britain joining the scheme .
The aim of the rules is to curb subsidised Chinese imports by giving EU-made products preferential treatment, but the UK and others such as Norway are worried about being left at a disadvantage if excluded from the scheme.
The price for joining would be aligning with the EU’s tariffs on Chinese EVs imposed by the bloc in 2024, according to a Franco-German proposal on Thursday night that said the UK would have to dynamically align with EU trade defence measures.
The Chinese embassy in London said it was “firmly opposed to any discriminatory practice involving tariff hikes or restrictive measures on Chinese products”. “We have expressed serious concern to the UK side regarding the reports in question,” it said, adding that “trade protectionism runs counter to WTO rules and market principles”.
This week, the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, said he would not be coerced into aligning with the EU’s policy.
However, the government has been desperate to be included in the Made in Europe package, fearing billions of pounds of trade in the car industry could be lost if the UK is locked out of supply chains in the EU.
Asked whether the UK accepted it would have to put tariffs on Chinese-made vehicles in order to join Made in Europe, a No 10 spokesperson said it was “premature to speculate” on the terms of any deal with the bloc and there was “still a European process to run”.
They added: “But more broadly, on the principle, the UK obviously has its own trade policy and it keeps all tariffs under review. And we work closely with the British automotive sector to make sure that that approach reflects their best interests.”
Chinese EVs are increasingly popular, with BYD sales up 78% year on year in September, Chery up 660% and the lesser-known Changan up by more than 3,000% in terms of market share.
EU lawmakers are expected to finalise the Industrial Accelerator Act, known as Made in Europe legislation, by the end of the year or early 2027.
But MEPs have already tabled 5,100 amendments, including one embracing the UK and giving Andy Burnham time to secure the deal he wants.
Earlier this week the boss of Mercedes-Benz, Ola Källenius, who is also the president of the European car trade body ACEA, warned that locking the UK out of legislation would amount to a “deliberate choice” by EU leaders to “hurt” the car industry across the bloc.
According to the new Franco-German proposal, there would be “an opt-in to further include European partners who were part of the EU single market as of 1 January 2020”, which includes the UK and Norway.
This would be provided those third countries accepted “dynamic alignment on the EU’s conditions related to third countries’ investments and on relevant EU trade defence measures”.
Tariffs could help UK-based manufacturers by preventing cut-price Chinese models flooding the market but they could also push up prices for consumers and harm British manufacturers trying to sell vehicles to China in the case of an escalating trade war. About 80% of UK-made cars are exported, with more than half going to the EU and 6% to China.
Earlier on Thursday the trade minister, Anas Sarwar, hinted that the UK was minded to align on tariffs. He told Politico the UK and the EU must “work together and act in lockstep” to tackle China’s dominance in the automotive sector.
A car industry source said the EU “has recently shown that it is possible to have a dialogue with the Chinese and get some form of safeguarding in place” without retaliation.
China opposes the expansion of EV tariffs. In the past few months it has made what European Commission officials called “bloodcurdling threats” to launch a trade war over the latest plan to impose quotas on Chinese hybrid cars.
While quotas can be introduced within months under World Trade Organization rules, it could take more than a year to impose tariffs on Chinese cars, with strict processes to be followed, starting with notification of an investigation and followed by evidence-gathering and sharing over alleged harms China might be causing to the British car industry.
Liam Byrne, the Labour chair of the parliamentary business committee, has said imposing tariffs on Chinese EVs would be “a small price to pay” to save the industry in both the UK and the EU.
At a conference in London on Thursday night, he said the UK “urgently needs” a new strategy on China to ensure that British and European manufacturing “does not die”.
Byrne, who has been leading an investigation into the UK’s position on China, was highly critical of the government’s approach, which he believes is naive and based on false hopes that China will change its export policy.
“Our China strategy is simply not where it needs to be. The UK urgently needs a coherent China strategy, which it does not have today,” he said.

articles.title_orig: AI Fears Return With Data Center Firm Elice’s 33% Debut Flop
articles.title_zh: AI Fears Return With Data Center Firm Elice’s 33% Debut Flop
articles.content_orig:
Shares in South Korean AI services firm Elice Group plummeted 30% in their market debut on Tuesday, amid a sharp retreat in sentiment towards the sector that has also derailed other planned listings.
Elice, which raised 201.1 billion won ($150 million) in its IPO, provides AI cloud services as well as AI-based education and business software and plans to spend most of its IPO proceeds on launching portable modular data centers and related infrastructure.
Investors are increasingly questioning whether massive AI spending can pay off anytime soon as elevated inflation keeps borrowing costs high.
Analysts noted that Elice's IPO had been priced on Oct. 6, before the recent sell-off in AI-related stocks.
"Elice's debut shows the AI infrastructure trade has moved from 'build at any cost' to 'who is paying and for how long'," said Ke Yan, head of research at Singapore-based Shenton Research.
"Until the AI labs that rent ... capacity show they can fund their compute commitments, new listings across the region will likely be priced in that risk premium."
This month, data center firms that have shelved their IPO plans include Australia's Firmus, which is backed by Nvidia, Blackstone-backed AirTrunk, which postponed a Singapore REIT IPO, as well as SB Energy, a unit of Japanese tech investment conglomerate SoftBank, which had filed paperwork for a U.S. IPO.
"Everyone is not sure how much demand for AI there will be and it is hard to estimate current demand," added Kim Hak-joon, an analyst at Seoul-based Kiwoom Securities.
Elice's shares were last trading at 63,600 won compared with its IPO pricing of 90,500 won. The IPO drew institutional orders worth 388.84 times the shares available in the offering, according to a filing.
The company has said revenue for the first half of the year tripled to 34 billion won and that it swung to an operating profit of 10 billion won compared with a 3.5 billion won loss for the same period a year earlier.

articles.title_orig: Scoop: Pete Hegseth meets with Netanyahu in Israel ahead of elections
articles.title_zh: Scoop: Pete Hegseth meets with Netanyahu in Israel ahead of elections
articles.content_orig:
United States Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has met Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu during an undisclosed visit to Israel, according to Axios.
The meeting between the hawkish ally of US President Donald Trump and the veteran Israeli premier facing a knife-edge election occurred on Monday, Axios reported, citing two sources with knowledge of the matter.
A spokesman for the US Department of Defense told Al Jazeera it “declines to comment” on the report.
Hegseth wrote on a social media post that he had visited US service members in the Central Command area of responsibility, which covers the Middle East, North Africa, and parts of Asia.
Israel’s Army Radio reported his meeting with Netanyahu took place at an air force base in Israel’s southern desert.
The reports of the visit come a day after President Trump took to his social media platform Truth Social to endorse Netanyahu in next week’s parliamentary election, the first vote since the Hamas-led October 7 attacks in 2023 and Israel’s genocidal campaign in Gaza.
Trump praised the prime minister for being an ally of the US in its war on Iran. He added that Netanyahu had his “Complete and Total Endorsement”.
“BIBI NETANYAHU WILL NEVER LET YOU DOWN!” Trump wrote.
Netanyahu’s religious-nationalist coalition is projected to lose its governing majority, although the opposition may also struggle to form a government, opinion polls suggest.
US Vice President JD Vance, however, declined to endorse Netanyahu in an interview earlier on Monday, saying he was not getting involved in Israeli elections.
“I endorse American candidates, and that’s where I’m focused on is the midterms,” Vance, who travelled to Budapest and endorsed Viktor Orban in Hungarian elections earlier this year, said in an interview with digital media outlet 2WAY.
“I’m not anti-endorsing him, but I’m not pro-endorsing him; I’m not getting involved in Israeli elections,” Vance said.

articles.title_orig: What we know about Australian MP hit by car in apparent deliberate attack
articles.title_zh: What we know about Australian MP hit by car in apparent deliberate attack
articles.content_orig:
Australian independent MP Helen Haines is in hospital in a critical condition after she was struck by a car outside her electorate office in what Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said appears to have been "a deliberate act".
The incident in Wangaratta, north-east of Melbourne, happened on Monday afternoon local time.
Albanese said counter-terrorism police are involved in the investigation.
Haines was struck by a White Toyota Landcruiser outside her electorate office on Monday.
The driver allegedly reversed to run into her a second time, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said.
"What witnesses have described is the driver doing a U-turn to get into the car park and to ram Helen against a vehicle, then to reverse and do it a second time," Burke told national broadcaster ABC on Tuesday morning.
A local barber Ricky Jefferies said he heard a loud commotion and ran towards the car, telling reporters on Tuesday that took a knife off the driver.
He said that multiple people "got involved immediately" to stop the alleged attacker.
Haines was airlifted to a Melbourne hospital where she underwent surgery.
She has lost one of her legs, according to local media. National broadcaster the Australian Broadcasting Corporation report that surgeons are working to save her other leg.
Victoria Police arrested the driver of the car, a 43-year-old man from the nearby town of Tarrawingee.
Local media reports have named the suspect as Brendan Nugent. Police have not confirmed the name of the man arrested.
Few details have been shared about Nugent, although he reportedly campaigned widely on environmental issues, including advocating against logging.
He was was detained at the scene by a passer-by before being taken into custody by officers, police said.
A knife was also seized, according to officers.
Victoria Police said it was unknown whether the suspect and Haines knew each other and its investigation remains ongoing.
On Tuesday morning Albanese said the suspect drove past Haines and did a U-turn "in order to get back" to where she was before hitting her with the car.
"It's clear this was a deliberate act," he told the ABC, adding it was not an "accident".
The motive for the attack is not clear, he said, and police are continuing their investigations.
Haines is a 65-year-old Independent MP for the Indi division in Victoria, south-eastern Australia.
She grew up in the south west of Victoria on a dairy farm with four brothers before training as a nurse and a midwife.
She became the matron of the Chiltern Bush Nursing Hospital in Victoria when she was 26, before later completing a master's degree in public health and a PhD in Medical Science while raising her three children and working, according to her website. She lives with her family on a small cattle farm outside Wangaratta.
The MP was first elected to the Australian House of Representatives in 2019 and was re-elected in 2022 and 2025.
Haines's family said the incident happened outside her electorate office in Wangaratta, a city of about 30,000 people, a few hours north-east of Melbourne in the state of Victoria.
Police said she was hit outside an office on Murphy Street at about 15:35 local time (05:35 BST).
Albanese appeared close to tears during a live television interview on ABC's 7.30 programme when he was asked if Australian politicians talk among themselves about the threats and risks they face.
"Yes," he replied, adding: "My concern at this point in time is for one of my colleagues."
He later described how there had been a "rise in temperature" and "too much shouting, not enough discourse" in Australia.
Speaking in a news conference, Australian Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said there had been an increase in reports of harassing and threatening behaviour towards lawmakers in the 2025-26 financial year, compared with 951 for the previous year.
Paying tribute to Haines during a news conference, Albanese described her as "incredibly hard-working".
"She is fiercely intelligent but most importantly she is just a thoroughly decent human being full of integrity and respected right across the Parliament and from everyone who comes into contact with her", he added.
He said the attack will come as an "incredible shock" to her community.
Australia's Foreign Minister Penny Wong described the incident as a "shocking and deeply disturbing attack".
The Premier of Victoria Ben Carroll said he was "deeply appalled" by the "violent attack".
Meanwhile, Australia's opposition leader Angus Taylor said he was "deeply saddened and distressed" by the attack.
"This is a shocking day for our nation," he said. "No-one should be targeted in this way."
But MPs from a range of political backgrounds have also described feeling deeply concerned about their safety in recent times: wearing disguises in public, locking their office doors, and scanning every crowd for potential threats.

articles.title_orig: Bari Weiss Derangement Syndrome
articles.title_zh: Bari Weiss Derangement Syndrome
articles.content_orig:
Phillips sought to buck up his fellow London bureau colleagues during a contentious staff meeting on Tuesday
The veteran British broadcaster Sir Trevor Phillips had some strong words of advice for his CBS News colleagues when facing off against critics who question the editorial integrity of the network: “Why don’t you just fuck off and let us do our jobs?”
Phillips made his blunt suggestion during a contentious meeting of the network’s London bureau on Tuesday, during which the foreign editor, Shayndi Raice, went on a lengthy tirade criticizing unnamed staffers for suggesting that editorial oversight amounted to “interference” and informing colleagues that disobeying editors would be insubordination and “legal grounds for firing”.
Phillips’s decision to join CBS was announced in June . It came after its billionaire owner, David Ellison, installed the opinion journalist and broadcast newcomer Bari Weiss as editor-in-chief in a move that shook staff .
The Guardian, which first reported the Tuesday meeting, reviewed an audio recording of the contentious session that rattled staffers. A CBS News spokesperson and Phillips declined to comment on the meeting.
Phillips spoke up initially to defend Raice, saying that the message she was delivering was common sense. “I’m genuinely surprised that you had to say anything that you just said in the last 15 minutes,” he said during the meeting. “It just seems to be axiomatic in any organization … I did want to say that I’m kind of surprised that in an organization of this vintage and capability, with the clever people I’ve met around here, that any of this actually has to be said.”
He then turned to outside opinion about CBS, telling colleagues that he faced criticism after it was announced he was leaving his perch at Sky News to serve as the network’s senior global affairs correspondent. Phillips is also a contributor to CBS’s flagship news show 60 Minutes, and voiced a short piece on Sunday on protests in Europe. Since CBS parent Paramount Global was acquired by Ellison’s Skydance Media in the summer of 2025, the company’s leadership has faced accusations of tilting the editorial scales in a more conservative-friendly direction.
“I could spend the next hour telling you the number of people when it was announced that I was coming here, the number of people who told me for all of the reasons you just explained, why this is the end of my career and how I was going to destroy everything that I’ve ever created, and all of that bollocks,” Phillips said.
He continued: “I think we’re in a new game now, actually, where we are now players as journalists. And what people are constantly trying to do is to knock us off – to frighten us, essentially, into doing this or doing that. It puts a premium on two things – one is our objectivity, and two: having each other’s backs. I think the worst thing that can happen now is if we start to go about telling people, ‘Well, I would have done this if the higher-ups hadn’t told me to do that.’ That’s exactly what everybody wants us to get into the game of. That’s how we become vulnerable. That’s how we start adjusting our copy according to somebody else’s lines outside of here … I think what you said is really, really important, but it points me in the direction of us having the mentality – forgive my French here – of telling everybody, ‘Why don’t you just fuck off and let us do our jobs?’”

articles.title_orig: Morning Bid: Korean canary in the AI coalmine
articles.title_zh: Morning Bid: Korean canary in the AI coalmine
articles.content_orig:
South Korea's AI-stock rout deepened Tuesday as Elice, a cloud-infrastructure company, crashed 32% in its market debut.
The benchmark Kospi index closed 4% lower, despite a rebound in Wall Street tech stocks on Monday. Index heavyweights Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix fell 3% and 4%, respectively.
South Korean chipmakers are major suppliers of memory used in AI systems, making their shares a closely watched gauge of the global AI boom.
The Kospi's latest selloff marks another blow for a market that has swung from boom to a nearly 40% bust in just four months.
The turmoil has also hit companies hoping to capitalize on the AI boom.
Elice, a South Korean company that rents out computing power for AI workloads, closed at 61,500 won on the Kosdaq, far below its IPO price of 90,500 won. The company raised about 201 billion won, or $151 million, in the Kosdaq's largest IPO this year.
The company's disastrous debut came despite overwhelming demand, with institutional and retail subscriptions topping available shares by roughly 400 times.
But Elice's IPO valued it far more richly than similar AI cloud companies, whose shares had already lost 20% to 60% over the preceding month, Tan wrote.
Similar concerns are rippling through AI infrastructure markets well beyond South Korea.
Take a smarter break in your day - and see how far you get.
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
US-listed CoreWeave, which rents AI computing power, saw its shares and bonds tumble last week amid concern about its debt-fueled expansion. Nvidia-backed Firmus, meanwhile, withdrew its planned $5 billion Australian IPO, citing volatile market conditions.

articles.title_orig: Asia stocks slump as AI jitters hammer Korean chipmakers ahead of tech earnings
articles.title_zh: Asia stocks slump as AI jitters hammer Korean chipmakers ahead of tech earnings
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
By Caroline Valetkevitch and Danilo Masoni
NEW YORK/MILAN, Oct 19 (Reuters) - The Nasdaq rose more than 1% on Monday as tech shares rebounded ahead of a big week for AI-related earnings, while European stocks and the euro fell as unrest in France added to concerns about the country's fiscal outlook.
French bonds and Paris-listed ‌stocks also fell as the widespread protests across France underscored the difficulties the government faces in reducing its large deficit.
France's central government asked some local authorities to ‌impose curfews as it faced pressure over security failings on Monday, after looting stemming from the protests.
Tech stocks on Wall Street recovered some ground after a bruising week, with an index of semiconductors up 1.6%. On Friday, the index ​sank in its eighth straight day of declines, its longest losing streak since 2008.
With results due from Meta on Wednesday, and results from Tesla and chipmakers Lam Research and Texas Instruments also due this week, investors will be watching for signs that massive AI spending ultimately pays off.
"Investors are buying the correction dip that we had," said Peter Cardillo, chief market economist at Spartan Capital Securities in New York.
"The market is now going to go through a very critical test over the next two weeks. We have some big-name earnings coming out," he said. "In terms of technology, the test ‌of whether or not the spending on AI... will be met ⁠with satisfaction is going to be critical."
The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 36.38 points, or 0.07%, to 51,966.03, the S&P 500 rose 31.29 points, or 0.41%, to 7,690.73 and the Nasdaq Composite rose 290.85 points, or 1.11%, to 26,430.89. MSCI's gauge of stocks across the globe rose 0.88 points, ⁠or 0.08%, to 1,129.98.
Meta is one of five AI hyperscalers expected to increase combined capital expenditure to about $1.2 trillion next year, according to Goldman Sachs.
Results from SpaceX are also due on Tuesday. Overall, US earnings are still expected to rise about 30%, largely driven by growth in the technology sector.
US Treasury yields rose on Monday, with the benchmark 10-year Treasury yield coming off its biggest weekly drop in seven ​months, ​as concerns about the impact of higher interest rates on AI stocks abated. The yield on the benchmark ​US 10-year Treasury note was up 4.2 basis points at 5.14%.
The recent ‌bond selloff had also intensified scrutiny of the AI sector's massive funding needs.
In economic data, the National Association of Home Builders/Wells Fargo Housing Market index on Monday showed a drop of three points to 29 this month, the lowest level since June 2012 and below the 31 estimate of economists polled by Reuters.
Recent comments from Federal Reserve officials, including Chair Kevin Warsh, suggest policymakers are in no rush to hike rates again. On Friday, Warsh expressed optimism about US economic strength but gave no indication of whether or when more hikes will be needed.
EUROPEAN STOCKS, EURO FALL
The pan-European STOXX 600 index fell 0.8%, while France's blue-chip CAC 40 index dropped 1.1%.
France's 10-year yield earlier was up 13 basis points to 4.9% while the German 10-year yield, the ‌benchmark for the euro zone, was also higher. The spread between French OATs and safe-haven German Bunds ​has widened to 147 basis points, trading at levels last seen during the 2011 to 2012 European debt crisis, ​from around 110 bps in late September.
Widespread weekend unrest in the euro zone's second-largest ​economy underscored the challenge facing the French government as it seeks to reduce its large budget deficit ahead of next year's presidential elections.
The euro ‌fell 0.24% to $1.1212.
The US dollar was boosted by the rebound in tech ​stocks. The dollar index, which measures the greenback against ​a basket of currencies including the yen and the euro, rose 0.17% to 101.97.
Meanwhile, the Australian dollar rose 0.49% versus the greenback after data showed China's economic growth rebounded from three-year lows, expanding at a 4.5% annual pace in the third quarter.
Oil prices were mixed, with investors digesting attacks by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis on a Yemeni military training ​camp and renewed attacks on Saudi energy, airport and military facilities.
Brent ‌crude futures fell 31 cents to settle at $109.55 a barrel. Brent fell more than $3 earlier in the session.
US West Texas Intermediate gained $2.25 to $103.66 a barrel, the highest ​settlement since September 15.
Spot gold fell 0.61% to $4,139.67 an ounce.
(Reporting by Caroline Valetkevitch in New York and Danilo Masoni in Milan; additional reporting by Wayne Cole ​and Avinash P; Editing by Stephen Coates, Kevin Buckland, Xevi Fontdegloria, Nick Zieminski and Deepa Babington)

articles.title_orig: China’s new 0.1-nanometre electron microscope ready to challenge US and Japan
articles.title_zh: China’s new 0.1-nanometre electron microscope ready to challenge US and Japan
articles.content_orig:
Model marks shift from R&D to commercialisation and aligns with country’s effort to cut reliance on imported tech
China is ready to commercialise a 200-kilovolt transmission electron microscope with an information resolution down to 0.1 nanometres that could introduce a new challenger into a market long dominated by the US and Japan.
Developed by Hefei-based manufacturer CIQTEK, the microscope features a point resolution of 0.25nm and an information limit of 0.1nm – on par with leading workhorse models on the market.
This marks a shift for the country’s expanding advanced electron microscopy industry from research and development to commercialisation, according to a report by the official ministry newspaper Science and Technology Daily on Monday.
It also represents the latest achievement aimed at reducing the country’s reliance on imports of the technology used in vital advanced industries like chip manufacturing.
